(Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals went to work on fixing one of the NFL’s worst defenses from last season. They made a number of moves, but according to one analyst, it was nowhere near enough. Warren Sharp from Sharp Football Analysis has ranked Cincinnati’s front seven 26th in the NFL : The Bengals overhauled their struggling front seven, but it’s hard to imagine the pass-rush unit drastically improving after the loss of Trey Hendrickson. Last season, Cincy generated pressure in 2.5 seconds or less on just 15% of opponent dropbacks, ranked 31st. The addition everyone knows is their trade for defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence from the New York Giants. But that wasn’t the only move the team made to improve that area. The Bengals also signed pass rusher Boye Mafe, who was one of the top available players at his position as well. He generated 40 pressures last season in a rotational role. They also landed Jonathan Allen to help the interior defense as well. He can add some help getting to the quarterback. The linebackers definitely needed a reliable veteran added to the group. Demetrius Knight and Barrett Carter had really rough rookie years. They were also surrounded by one of the worst defensive units in the NFL. Still, that would definitely keep them from being too high on this list. Speaking of the list, though. There are quite a few issues that need to be pointed out that are directly tied to the Bengals. Truly, if all the Bengals did was lose Hendrickson and add Lawrence, there wouldn’t have been too much movement up, but there should have been at least a minor boost. When you look at Sharp’s 2025 rankings for front sevens , you will find something strange. Cincinnati was ranked 26th last year as well. But Sharp also mentioned two names in his analysis, Lawrence and Henderickson. So, how did those players impact the rank of their former and new teams? Well, the Giants fell 14 spots from No. 4 to No. 18. Somehow, the loss of Lawrence is worth absolutely tanking a unit, but adding him means nothing. Although the Bengals lost Hendrickson, obviously, he must have also had a huge impact, right? Well, maybe too much of an impact. Sharp ranks the Baltimore Ravens as the 10th best in the NFL. He even notes the defensive line was at or near the bottom of the NFL last year. Somehow, adding Hendrickson, Calais Campbell, and Zion Young makes it a top 10 unit. Hendrickson also isn’t going to be very helpful in improving that running defense. He is still a fantastic pass rusher, but anyone watching Bengals games knew the offensive plan included running right at him. And unfortunately, with his age, he likely won’t be getting better in that area. So, somehow saying the Lawrence move is equal to the Hendrickson one just seems silly and disingenuous. There is plenty of uncertainty surrounding this Bengals defensive unit, but it is really hard to make this math work out for everyone except Cincinnati.

Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns walked off the field on January 13, 2024, at Houston’s NRG Stadium, disappointed but with the belief that better days were ahead. Cleveland had just fallen to the Houston Texans in a Wild Card playoff game, the second playoff appearance in four years for the Browns. That offseason, head coach Kevin Stefanski picked up his second Coach of the Year Award, providing hope that after so many years wandering in the NFL’s wasteland, playoff appearances were going to be a frequent occurrence. Everyone knows how that all worked out as the Browns won a total of eight games over the next two seasons, leading to Stefanski being fired and general manager Andrew Berry starting on the latest rebuilding project. Those past two seasons stood out while reading Vic Tafur’s latest article at The Athletic , in which he predicts a “best bet” for each of the league’s 32 teams for the upcoming season. As it relates to the Browns, Tafur is going with the over on Cleveland’s expected win total of 5.5 games from BetMGM, writing that: I have no faith in Deshaun Watson or Shedeur Sanders, but I like the rest of the offense, and there is still some defensive talent even after the Myles Garrett trade. The main reason to take the over is that the Browns are starting to stack great draft classes, and that’s rare in this league. Tafur is on the right track in highlighting the improvement at some key positions on offense, as well as a defense that boasts talent, even if none of that talent is on the level of Garrett. (No shame in that.) And the Browns did reach five wins last season, although the final two were the result of the Pittsburgh Steelers caring more about Garrett than winning and the greatest six-point offensive explosion in NFL history. But the six wins needed to hit the over also represent almost as many victories as the Browns had combined in the past two seasons. It does not seem impossible – which is why the casinos always win in Las Vegas – but there are still some major concerns about this team: No matter who the starter is, the quarterback room remains the unquestioned worst in the NFL . No one knows just how well the rebuilt offensive line will play until they actually get on the field together. If that goes poorly, the other areas of the offense that were improved will be for naught. The defense should still be fine even if Jared Verse is not Myles Garrett , but it would also not be a surprise if the unit sees a dip in its production. This is Todd Monken’s first time as a head coach. He may be Sean McVay or Matt LaFleur, but he could also be Bud Carson. Again, no one knows until they see him in action. This is one of those times as a Browns fan when you hope to be wrong, but hitting the under on wins feels like a far better bet at the moment. What do you think? Would you take the over on 5.5 wins or not? Let everyone know in the comments!

summary: Cowboys’ turnaround at key position hinges on a series of gambles – Jason Kandel, The Landry Hat The cornerback position is far from locked down. full_text: Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown makes a catch against Dallas Cowboys safety Malik Hooker (28) and cornerback DaRon Bland (26) during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Thursday, Dec. 4, 2025. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Cowboys’ turnaround at key position hinges on a series of gambles – Jason Kandel, The Landry Hat The cornerback position is far from locked down. Dallas is lucky they brought in DB guru Christian Parker to be their new defensive coordinator and work with these guys, but red flags are still flying. Let’s start with Bland, because his inability to stay healthy has plagued this defense across the last two seasons, and he will still play a key role. It wasn’t long ago that the 27-year-old led the NFL with nine interceptions (and five pick-sixes) in 2023, but he’s only played 19 games in the two years since. Recent history suggests that the $92 million man can’t stay healthy. And he did not participate in offseason activities. And then there’s Durant, who was one of the bigger free-agent signings the Cowboys made this offseason. While he was a solid starter in Los Angeles last season, he has some issues of his own, so the Rams were quick to cast him aside in favor of Jaylen Watson and Trent McDuffie. The fifth-year cornerback is far from a sure thing. According to Pro Football Focus, Durant’s 66.8 PFF grade ranked 39th out of 114 qualified CBs , while his 67.4 coverage grade ranked 37th. However, he allowed an 85.6 passer rating when targeted, and is also pretty below average as a run defender. Then there’s Revel, who’s facing similar question marks to both of them. The 2025 third-round pick out of East Carolina missed the first 10 games of last season while rehabbing from the ACL tear that ended his college career. And once he returned, it got worse for him, as he played at less than 100%. 6 under-the-radar Cowboys who could shock in 2026 training camp – K.D. Drummond, Cowboys Wire Keep an eye on these names you may have forgotten about. OT Ajani Cornelius There’s no secret that the Dallas Cowboys have a really strong offense. As long as QB Dak Prescott is healthy, the team routinely finds themselves in, or in close proximity to, top-5 ranking in many metrics for that side of the ball. The one roster weakness they have there, though, is at the tackle position. Neither Tyler Guyton nor Terence Steele inspire visions of Pro Bowl appearances or All-Pro accolades. Most conversations around who could challenge them are centered around Nate Thomas or this year’s fourth-round pick Drew Shelton.Expert NFL picks: Exclusive betting insights only at USA TODAY. But perhaps Cornelius, who is in the same position this season as Thomas was last year, could shockingly join the conversation. The No. 204 selection from 2025 out of Oregon, Cornelius was identified by this current staff as someone they hoped to develop. There are several people in his way, but the climb to the top isn’t nearly as steep as other positions. TE Michael Trigg There’s no question about it, the tight end in Dallas’ offense has been fed as a result of whatever else is happening on the field. Jake Ferguson is a good outlet, but he’s not a dominating force and gives nothing after the catch. His fumbling issues has made him even less of a compliment. His backups leave a lot to be desired as pass catchers, meaning that if there’s anyone with juice at the position, they have a chance to contribute. The question for Trigg isn’t about juice; he’s a plus-level pass catcher… like highlight reel worthy pass catchter. The question is whether or not he can do the rest of the job description for being a professional tight end, and whether he can do that in the matter of one offseason. He went undrafted for those reasons, can he turn things around and become the shock player of this year’s camp. Cowboys Dubbed Logical Landing Spot for All-Pro Who May Be Final Piece to the Puzzle – Mike Moraitis, Sports Illustrated There’s still time to add depth. Despite all of their moves, Bleacher Report’s Kristopher Knox is of the opinion the Cowboys should make one more addition to their linebackers room by signing Bobby Wagner . “At this stage in his career, Wagner would make the most sense for a team seeking both talent and experience on its defense and with enough overall talent to make a strong push for the postseason,” Knox wrote. “Logical Landing Spots: Dallas Cowboys, Jacksonville Jaguars,” Knox added. Cowboys’ current situation at linebacker The Cowboys had a dire situation at the position going into the offseason, but things have improved since then. Dallas traded for Dee Winters before opting to select Jaishawn Barham in the third round of the 2026 NFL Draft, and those two join a linebackers room that also includes both DeMarvion Overshown and Shemar James. While that should be an adequate group, there are questions about each player in it. Overshown has been plagued by injury during his career, Barham and James are unproven and Winters amounts to an OK but not great starting option. If there’s one position group that could use a final piece to put it over the top, it’s linebacker. Christian Parker’s Hire Follows a Cowboys Super Bowl Pattern – Cody Warren, Inside The Star Fans have to hope history repeats itself. Ernie Stautner, Dave Wannstedt, Butch Davis, and Dave Campo all led defenses during Super Bowl seasons . We know those names now because of what came later, but it doesn’t mean each one arrived as some famous NFL coordinator everybody wanted. Stautner built his reputation with the defensive line under Tom Landry. Wannstedt followed Jimmy Johnson from the University of Miami and got his first NFL coaching job in Dallas. Davis worked his way up through the defensive front. Campo climbed through the secondary. Dallas didn’t always chase the hottest name available, but instead trusted coaches who were still moving up and gave them a defense before the rest of the league knew who they were. I think that’s where I’m at on the Christian Parker hire. He’s getting his chance because the coaches and players who have been around him knew he was ready for more, not because he bounced around collecting coordinator titles. I think we can all get behind that aspect of it easier than another recycled hire everybody knows. Daily discussion question: What is the ceiling on this team in your opinion?

Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images | Chris Jones-Imagn Images The Dallas Cowboys offense and defense were near polar opposites a season ago. While they were one of the best offensive units in the league last year, they were also historically bad on the defensive side of the ball, arguably the worst in the NFL. We all knew big changes are coming at the end of the 2025 season, but none of us knew exactly how much. Now, heading into training camp, we all know the Cowboys have been much an entire new defensive coaching staff, headlined by a first-time ever defensive coordinator, Christian Parker. He’s installing a new, versatile 3-4 scheme and added several new faces to the roster to align more than what he prefers at each individual position. How this all plays out as the ultimate mystery. There seems to be an endless amount of unanswered questions about the Cowboys defense heading into training camp, but sitting at the top of the list has to be the overall depth at the linebacker position. It was a sore spot for them a season ago, which is why we’re likely to see an entirely new faces manning the position this year. As things stand right now, it looks as if DeMarvion Overshown is the favored option to start at the MIKE LB position. He’s entering a contract year and has missed a total of 32 games in his three seasons with the Cowboys due to two separate season-ending knee injuries. If he can overcome his injuries and stay healthy, he’s shown glimpses of game-changing ability. Expected to start next to Overshown at the WILL LB position is Dee Winters who the Cowboys acquired via trade from the San Francisco 49ers for a fifth-round pick. He’s someone they had an eye on since coming out of TCU and finally pulled the trigger to bring him aboard. He’s started 27 games last two years, making him the most seasoned LB on the roster. Overshown and Winters have a chance to be a much improved LB duo for the Cowboys than any kind the combination they deployed last year. However, neither has much experience playing 3-4 scheme, causing a little bit of concern. That is what training camp, to see if they are able to seamlessly transition into the scheme and flourish. Behind them, the LB depth he’s even more of a mystery, starting with this year’s third-round pick Jaishawn Barham. If anybody challenges Overshown for the starting MIKE LB position, it might be the rookie out of Michigan. His physicality and versatility as an off-ball LB and pass rusher could put him in contention for a starting role if he shows up in training camp. And we can forget about last year’s leading tackler, Shemar James. No one knows what kind of role the second-year LB will play with Christian Parker running the show this year. Last year as a rookie he showed some good things on tape, but still needs to improve his game by leaps and bounds he wants to earn significant playing time this year. The rest of the Cowboys LB depth is probably competing just to make the final 53-man roster. If no one emerges from the pack, Dallas may look outside the organization in the hopes of finding an upgrade, whether it’s for depth purposes or for a potential starter. That of course remains to be seen, but something to keep in mind as things progress throughout training camp/preseason.

He was selected in the fifth round by Tampa Bay, joining the Bucs when Tom Brady became their starting quarterback. As a rookie, Johnson had a small role in the WR rotation but got to claim a Super Bowl ring. He had a larger share in 2021, 36 catches for 360 yards, but didn’t make it past final cuts the following season. In two years with Tampa, Johnson only sat for two games and got six starts. From there, Johnson bounced around the league a bit. The Texans claimed him off the Bucs’ waiver but barely played him in 2022, then released him in October. Tampa brought him back via the practice squad, but he didn’t get any action. In 2023, he started the offseason with the Raiders but ended up going to training camp with the Rams. Again, he didn’t make the roster and spent the year on their practice squad. Johnson returned with Los Angeles in 2024 and earned a reserve role, playing in 15 games and logging 291 yards on 26 catches. The following offseason, he signed with the Jets and played a bit role with 12 catches for 197 yards in just 12 games, though he did start five of them. Last April, the Cowboys came out of a mostly defense-focused draft with WR Anthony Smith as a seventh-round pick, and a couple of undrafted free agents. But with veteran Parris Campbell retiring, they sought more experienced depth options and signed Johnson, as well as Marquez Valdes-Scantling, to the 90-man roster. Contract Status Years Left: 1 2026 Cap Hit: $1.08 million Given his low NFL profile, and that he was still available after the draft, Johnson got an unsurprisingly minimal contract from Dallas. 2026 Projections Role: Backup WR Roster Chance: 15% As we’ve said before, three WR spots are locked in with your superstars and Ryan Flournoy, and then KaVontae Turpin should have a fourth for his return work and occasional offensive usage. That doesn’t leave much for the rest of the pack: two spots at best, but quite possibly just one more. That makes for a battle royal this summer between veterans like Johnson, Valdes-Scantling, and Jonathan Mingo against young prospects like Smith, Traeshon Holden, Jordan Hudson, and others. In a way, Johnson feels like the “middle” candidate in this field. He turns 28 in August, so he’s still right in that prime window. He doesn’t have Valdes-Scantling’s experience, but he’s also about four years younger. While he’s had some droughts in his playing time, he’s arguably accomplished more in the league than Mingo. If he takes to a new offense quickly, Johnson’s reliable hands and on-field toughness could help him compete. But if he is going to be WR4 or 5, a lack of proven special teams value could hurt. Johnson very much feels like classic veteran insurance. If CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, and Flournoy are all healthy and ready to start Week 1, then Johnson probably loses out to younger guys with more upside. But if there is a greater need for experienced receivers when the Cowboys travel to New York for the season opener, Johnson could get more consideration at final cuts. title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 56
summary: It is Day 56 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. full_text: It is Day 56 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. Let’s get ready for Day 56 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, when we revisit one of the wildest, most painful, and most unforgettable games of the Tony Romo era. The Broncos came to Arlington undefeated in 2013, with Peyton Manning playing at an MVP level in one of the greatest offensive seasons a quarterback has ever produced. The Cowboys entered at 2-2 and needed a statement win. What followed was less a football game and more a heavyweight quarterback duel. Sunday, October 6, 2013 — 4:25 p.m. ET AT&T Stadium, Arlington, Texas Final Score: Denver Broncos 51, Dallas Cowboys 48 Dallas started fast. Romo led an 11-play, 79-yard opening drive and found Dez Bryant for a two-yard touchdown. The Cowboys then forced a Denver fumble on the Broncos’ first possession, and DeMarco Murray punched in a four-yard touchdown to put Dallas up 14-0. For a moment, it looked like the Cowboys might actually control the game by keeping Manning on the sideline. That idea did not last. Manning answered with a quick touchdown pass to Julius Thomas, then Denver scored 21 straight points in the second quarter. Eric Decker caught a short touchdown, Thomas added another, and then Manning produced one of the funniest plays of his career, faking the entire defense before bootlegging into the end zone for a rare rushing touchdown. Dallas added a late Dan Bailey field goal, but the Broncos led 28-20 at halftime. The third quarter looked like it might get away from Dallas when Manning hit Wes Welker for a two-yard touchdown to make it 35-20. Then Romo went nuclear. He hit rookie Terrance Williams for an 82-yard touchdown. Later, he found Bryant again from two yards out. Morris Claiborne then intercepted Manning, ending Manning’s streak of 227 passes without a pick, and Romo immediately turned that into a 10-yard touchdown to Jason Witten. Dallas had gone from down 35-20 to leading 41-38. The fourth quarter, however, was when the insanity peaked. Prater tied it at 41 with a 50-yard field goal, then Romo hit Bryant for a 79-yard gain to push him past 500 passing yards on the day. One play later, Romo found Cole Beasley for a four-yard touchdown, giving Dallas a 48-41 lead. Denver answered with a long drive of its own, capped by a one-yard Knowshon Moreno touchdown, tying the game at 48 just before the two minute warning. Then came the play that still hurts. With the game tied and Dallas backed up near its own goal line, Romo tried to fit a pass to Gavin Escobar. Broncos linebacker Danny Trevathan made a brilliant diving interception, giving Denver the ball in field-goal range. Manning milked the clock, Prater hit from 28 yards with two seconds left, and the Cowboys lost one of the greatest shootouts in NFL history. This game belongs on the countdown because some losses are too iconic to ignore. Cowboys fans remember the heartbreak, but they also remember Romo standing toe-to-toe with Peyton Manning at the peak of his powers and nearly beating him in a game where neither defense could breathe. It was spectacular, exhausting, unfair, and forever unforgettable. #Cowboys vs #Broncos 2013 Week 5 The Romo vs Manning game Final Score: Denver Broncos 51, Dallas Cowboys 48 #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/S8xxU8t2V5 — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) July 18, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game Romo’s 506 passing yards was the first 500-yard passing game in Cowboys history and broke Don Meredith’s previous franchise record of 460 yards, set in 1963. Romo’s 506 passing yards still remains a franchise record. title: 3 Cowboys who could become household names this season
summary: It is very difficult to be unknown or underrated while playing for the Dallas Cowboys. The team is covered at such great length and has a level of visibility that nobody can quite touch. To be clear nobody is saying that this is the most important quality, or an important one in general, for a […]
full_text: Nov 17, 2025; Paradise, Nevada, USA; Dallas Cowboys wide receiver Ryan Flournoy (19) reacts towards the stands as he leaves the field following a game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | Kirby Lee-Imagn Images It is very difficult to be unknown or underrated while playing for the Dallas Cowboys. The team is covered at such great length and has a level of visibility that nobody can quite touch. To be clear nobody is saying that this is the most important quality, or an important one in general, for a football team, but it is a reality for America’s Team as we all know. In this spirit most players on the Cowboys are what we will refer to in this conversation as “household names.” Most people have heard of the likes of Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, Quinnen Williams, you get the picture. Even in spite of the team’s popularity though, not every player on the team is quite at that level. Seasons can always change that though and here is a list of three players who could find themselves in that territory should things go right for them. Ryan Flournoy CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens understandably get a lot of love, but there is another wide receiver on the Cowboys who could have a breakout type season for the team in Ryan Flournoy. Sometimes things simply shake out weirdly when it comes to pass-catching options. Things work in a certain way, rhythms fall into place, and you blink your eyes and all of a sudden Laurent Robinson is having a season where he catches 11 touchdowns. Robinson is a great example of the way things can happen, but we all feel better about Flournoy’s prospect in the Cowboys offense than Jacksonville did with Laurent in theirs by the end. Flournoy could be the primary beneficiary of coverage going elsewhere, and given the fantasy football nature of the NFL, he could quickly become more well-known than he is currently. Jalen Thompson Caleb Downs is the name to know at safety and that makes sense. But so many people have (seemingly) glossed over the fact that Dallas handed out the biggest deal that they had in free agency since Brandon Carr this offseason, and they gave it to Jalen Thompson. This isn’t to say that Thompson is better than Downs. But the new defensive coordinator literally, this is what free agency is, hand-picked Thompson to patrol his secondary. Christian Parker’s pedigree of molding defensive backs into household names is well-established. Thompson could be the next one to follow that lead. Jaydon Blue Some of this is that Jaydon Blue played at a highly visible college in the University of Texas, and some of it is the fantasy football aspect of life that we talked about with Ryan Flournoy. There is another element to Jaydon Blue though in that he has the potential to rip off big plays. Fans who consume the Cowboys more casually, through RedZone, or maybe through highlights might learn of Blue if he is ripping off these bigger and longer touchdowns. That is a fast pass to household status and he might be the person on the team with the proper speed to take advantage of it. This pick holds the least amount of confidence, though. Blue lost favor with the coaching staff last year, and while the slate is clean for 2026, there is still a ways to go before the opportunities even exist. Do you agree with these candidates, or do you have any that we left off? Let us know what you think in the comments below.

title: Why 2025 NFC East standings are a bad predictor of 2026 standings
summary: Every summer, NFL fans ask the same question: How good will my team be this year? The answers usually fall into one of two camps. One side points to free agency, the draft, and coaching changes. The other points to last year’s record. Neither tells the whole story. Long before analytics became mainstream, baseball writer […]
full_text: Every summer, NFL fans ask the same question: How good will my team be this year? The answers usually fall into one of two camps. One side points to free agency, the draft, and coaching changes. The other points to last year’s record. Neither tells the whole story. Long before analytics became mainstream, baseball writer Bill James proposed six indicators that tended to predict whether teams would improve or decline from one season to the next. The indicators were designed for baseball, not football, but the underlying ideas apply remarkably well to the NFL. Some of these indicators are stronger than others. None should be treated as definitive. The NFL is an unusually noisy sport. Teams play only 17 games. Injuries swing seasons. One tipped interception can change a division race. That means even the best statistical indicators should be viewed as tendencies rather than predictions. Our goal today isn’t to predict the 2026 standings. It’s to identify the forces quietly pushing teams toward improvement, or regression, before the season begins. Let’s see what they say about the 2026 NFC East. 1: Not Every Win Is Created Equal One of the strongest predictors of future performance isn’t a team’s record, it’s its point differential. Wins matter, of course. But not all wins are equally convincing. A team that consistently outscored opponents by two touchdowns is usually more sustainable than a team that survived a string of one-score games. That’s why analysts often start with point differential rather than the standings. Point Differential The Pythagorean Formula estimates how many games a team should have won based solely on points scored and points allowed. If a team wins significantly more games than expected, history suggests some regression is likely. If it wins fewer games than expected, improvement often follows. The Commanders and Giants finished with fewer wins than their point differential deserved, and are likely to improve, even without major roster changes. This is one of the most reliable indicators we have, because point differential tends to be much more stable from year to year than win-loss record. Close Games: Winning Every Coin Flip Isn’t a Skill One-score games have an outsized impact on NFL standings. The difference between a 12-win season and a 9-win season is often just a handful of plays spread across four or five close games. While elite teams may consistently put themselves in position to win late, the outcome of those games is surprisingly volatile from year to year. It means extreme close-game performance is difficult to sustain. If a team’s record was built on an exceptional performance in close games, history suggests some of that success is likely to fade – and vice versa. These two indicators are stronger together than they are separately. If some of last year’s results were inflated by close-game luck, how much of the overall season should we expect to repeat? 2: Extreme Seasons Rarely Stay Extreme Every NFL fan believes last year’s record tells us something, especially if it’s a good record. And the record does tell us something. Just not as much as we tend to think. Every NFL season produces a handful of surprises. A team comes seemingly out of nowhere to win 13 games. Another falls from the playoffs to the bottom of the division. Teams improve, coaches innovate, and players develop, but extreme outcomes also tend to include an unusually large dose of good or bad fortune. Once that fortune fades, records often drift back toward the middle. That’s why the next two indicators focus less on what happened and more on how likely it is to happen again. Regression to the Mean Regression to the mean is one of the most misunderstood concepts in sports. It isn’t a force of nature pulling every team toward .500. It’s a statistical observation that extreme outcomes are often followed by less extreme ones because the original result was influenced by factors that are difficult to repeat. Think about a team that finishes 14-3. To reach that record, it probably needed a talented roster, good coaching, solid quarterback play, relatively good health, favorable turnover luck, and perhaps a couple of fortunate bounces in close games. It’s entirely possible that every one of those things happens again. It’s just unlikely. The same logic applies at the other end of the standings. A four-win team isn’t automatically destined to improve, but it doesn’t need everything to change in order to win six or seven games the following year. Simply returning to league-average health or turnover luck can make a meaningful difference. The approximation for regression is intentionally simple. summary: Biggest Question Nobody Is Asking About Dallas Cowboys & How They Answer It – Mike Moraitis, SI.com What is the biggest question on the Cowboys roster as they prepare to head to Oxnard? How will Christian Parker perform in first season as defensive coordinator? The early reviews for Parker have been very promising and show that he […]
full_text: Biggest Question Nobody Is Asking About Dallas Cowboys & How They Answer It – Mike Moraitis, SI.com What is the biggest question on the Cowboys roster as they prepare to head to Oxnard? How will Christian Parker perform in first season as defensive coordinator? The early reviews for Parker have been very promising and show that he no doubt has the dedication necessary to turn things around in Dallas. Based on what we have heard from players and coaches and what we’ve seen at spring practices, Parker is clearly a hard worker and is hands on with his players, something the Cowboys’ defenders appreciate. “I feel like that’s when you learn fully what the coach means,” Caleb Downs said. “To be able to get hands on and be able to do the drill with you, I feel like that’s a real positive.” “I can’t get the guy to leave the building,” head coach Brian Schottenheimer said of Parker. “I kind of see myself as a grinder… I’m always out before he is and I’m like, ‘Dude.’ He just loves it, man. Parker is also very popular with his players, as Schottenheimer noted when he told reporters that Parker “literally has a line of guys” waiting outside his office to talk to him on a daily basis. That’s important to note because it means guys are willing to go the extra mile for their coach and that will only help Dallas’ defense improve. While these are all great signs that the Cowboys have the right man for the job, none of them guarantee Parker will be a successful defensive coordinator, especially in Year 1. After all, we’ve seen promising coaches fail at a bigger role time and time again over the years. At the very least, first-time play-callers like Parker can struggle as they adjust to the new job. The good news is, Parker has learned from some of the best in the business during his coaching career and few first-year coaches are better prepared than he will be. Dallas Cowboys Player Profile: Jaishawn Barham clearly has a bigger role waiting for him than expected – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports Jaishawn Barham will play a much bigger role than expected in year one. The Cowboys picked Barham in the third round of the 2026 NFL Draft with the pick they acquired in the Osa Odighizuwa trade via the San Francisco 49ers. His role going into the preseason is expected to be linebacker, but the line is a little blurry. Throughout the draft process, many listed Barham as an edge rusher. Reasonably so, as that’s where he played his last year in Michigan. However, the Cowboys immediately made it clear they view him as an inside linebacker first, which is where he started his collegiate career. His versatility should earn him a role on Christian Parker’s defense right away (more on that later). The Cowboys said after the draft they viewed Barham as a prospect worthy of going in the top two rounds, so getting him in the third had to be a big win in the war room. During the offseason program, Barham trained with the inside linebackers. Putting Cowboys players in first-round pick value form – RJ Ochoa, Blogging the Boys An interesting look at the value of some of the players on the Cowboys roster. ESPN placed first-round pick value on certain Cowboys players The great Bill Barnwell took it upon himself recently to identify how many players on each NFL team carry the value of a first-round pick . The idea here is if said players were to ever be made available in some sort of trade, but obviously a lot of them listed (he did this for every team as noted) would never even reach that point. This is for fun. In Barnwell’s estimation there are five players on the Cowboys who could fetch a first-round pick and more. One first-round pick and more: G Tyler Booker, WR CeeDee Lamb, QB Dak Prescott, G Tyler Smith, DT Quinnen Williams. The Cowboys just sent this sort of haul to acquire Williams, and between Booker and Smith, they have the NFL’s best 1-2 punch at guard. Lamb’s contract, which pays the 2020 first-round pick like one of the highest-paid wideouts in the game, might begin to look worrisome if he’s unable to reach the heights we saw in 2023 again sometime soon. Prescott’s value would be a fascinating discussion in its own right if the Cowboys star ever chose to waive his no-trade clause. His four-year, $240 million extension is the most player-friendly contract in the league, and it’s a product of owner Jerry Jones mishandling Prescott’s initial run toward free agency in 2019 and 2020. I’m not sure other teams see Prescott as that caliber of quarterback, although his consistency on the field would appeal to franchises that haven’t been able to find a steady hand under center. Dallas Cowboys Training Camp Battles to Watch & Who is Most Likely to Be Cut – Randy Gurzi, SI.com Will there be any surprise cuts this offseason? RB2: Jaydon Blue, Malik Davis, Phil Mafah Javonte Williams has the RB1 job on lockdown after a breakout season in 2025, but the Cowboys still need to find someone who could be a reliable backup. Rookie Jaydon Blue was supposed to fill that role last year, but he never earned the trust of the coaching staff. Malik Davis ended up stepping in and played well, but this offseason he’s going to have to fend off Blue, who comes in with a new focus . There’s also fellow second-year back Phil Mafah, who was a fan-favorite during the preseason last year, but spent most of his rookie campaign on the IR. Dallas will give the younger backs every opportunity to win the battle, which makes Davis most likely to be cut. Even if he is, however, the Cowboys would be thrilled to have him back on the practice squad for added depth. When Super Bowl LXI comes around on February 14, 2027, it’ll be over 31 years since Dallas last hoisted the Lombardi trophy. Regardless of the results of years past, the expectation to be at the top of the NFL remains the same for Prescott, who will play his 11 th season with the Cowboys in 2026. “That’s the one thing I love about the Cowboys nation and being a player of the Cowboys is, it’s Super Bowl or bust,” Prescott said while speaking to fans during a virtual meet and greet alongside Cowboys rookie DB Caleb Downs. “And truthfully, that’s the only reason you play this game. title: Broncos Country foresees prolific passing from Nix
summary: As a rookie, Bo Nix threw for 3,775 yards. Last year, he slung it just shy of 4,000 yards. A few of us are predicting a steeper rise this season with 4,500 yards or more, and only […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - JANUARY 17: Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix (10) passes in the second quarter against the Buffalo Bills in the AFC Divisional Round game at Empower Field at Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images As a rookie, Bo Nix threw for 3,775 yards. Last year, he slung it just shy of 4,000 yards. In year three, Broncos Country predicts its young QB will break the 4,000-yard barrier, but perhaps just barely. A few of us are predicting a steeper rise this season with 4,500 yards or more, and only a few non-believers (just kidding) stayed in the 3000s. Truth be told, I voted with the majority here but am secretly hoping it’s a little less. I’ll explain… Since last week we found out that NFL execs and coaches believe Nix’s talent is in the bottom half of the league, compared to several QBs he outperformed last year — Josh Allen, Patrick Mahomes and Justin Herbert — I thought it would be fun to see how many yards those three threw for in their first three years (you’re welcome for this highly extensive research via profootballreference.com, lol). Allen: 2074 (2018); 3,089 (2019); 4,544 (2020). Mahomes: 5097 (2018, first full year playing); 4,031 (2019); 4,740 (2020). Herbert: 4,336 (2020); 5,014 (2021); 4,739 (2022). We all remember that Allen was supposedly approaching “bust” status before his third-year breakout, and he’s been pretty unstoppable since. But without as many receiving weapons last year, Allen ended with his third lowest number of passing yards, just behind his first two seasons in the league. Mahomes’ first three seasons were among his best ever for passing yards as the last two seasons have both been under 4,000 yards — another casualty of losing top receivers but clearly not a huge problem for him and the Chiefs’ offense. Herbert also has had a drop-off since years two and three, which featured his best years for number of yards passing. Not that any of these comparisons mean anything year to year or to Nix’s potential in year three, but they do highlight how irrelevant number of passing yards can be overall. Herbert’s lower passing yard seasons were also the Chargers’ best W-L records in a while, and Allen and Mahomes have led their teams to playoffs regardless of any passing milestones or achievements. J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey headline the Denver Broncos top two backs going into training camp. #DenverBroncos #BroncosCountry pic.twitter.com/jwDOpFOYnE — Locked On Broncos (@LockedOnBroncos) July 13, 2026 I always love an explosive passing game, but I do think a more prolific run game is important for the Broncos’ offense this season, so I’m hoping the total passing yards from Nix by the end of the season is under 4,000 if that means the rushing yard totals are up. In the past five seasons, the Broncos have hovered just under 2,000 rushing yards, while the top rushing teams in the league have been closer to 3,000. If Nix’s passing yards are below 4,000 but that means the running backs are getting closer to 2,500 yards rushing, I think this offense will be as explosive as it has been in a long time.

They have followed this same blueprint for multiple seasons now, and I would anticipate them doing it again this season. Prentice will give the Broncos a physical lead blocker who can open up running lanes for the Broncos’ backs while also helping out the team in other areas. He has proven to be a reliable option in short-yardage situations as a runner, can be a sneaky pass catcher, and can even come in on third downs as a pass blocker. On top of all that, he also contributes in multiple ways on special teams. He is a core player you need on your roster to do a lot of the dirty work that isn’t often recognized by the media and fans but is beloved by the coaching staff for that very reason. The running game was thriving early on in the season, but struggled after JK Dobbins went down with injury. However, with Dobbins back and healthy. RJ Harvey in year two, and rookie Jonah Coleman joining the mix, the Broncos figure to be a better running team this upcoming season. Final Thoughts There really isn’t too much else to say here. Prentice doesn’t have any real competition for his role, and if he makes it through the summer healthy, he figures to be the Broncos’ fullback this upcoming season. I liked what we saw from him last season when they did include him in the offense. He was reliable in short-yardage and can sneak out and gain a few yards as a receiver. However, what he does best won’t be as noticeable. He’ll need to open up running lanes for the backs, help get the running game going again, and contribute on special teams. You need a player like this on your roster, and the Broncos have a good one in Adam Prentice.

(Photo by Eric Thomas/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! Evan Engram’s first season with the Denver Broncos is best described as “meh.” It clearly wasn’t great by any stretch of the imagination. But it also wasn’t terrible. It was just “meh.” Engram finished his first season in Denver with 50 receptions for 461 yards and one touchdown. His best game came in the win over the Washington Commanders when he had six catches for 79 yards. For a guy with a 2026 salary cap hit of $14.1 million, the expectations are higher. Yet despite that, throughout the 2025 season, Engram never seemed to be a focal point of the offense. The Joker that Sean Payton talked so much about heading into the season and was one of the main reasons the Broncos signed the tight end. Engram’s playmaking ability and threat over the middle really weren’t utilized. As to why Engram was a passenger in the offense, it’s likely a combination of game planning, the offense, Bo Nix, and Engram. As training camp nears in Denver, how Engram is better utilized this season is one of the most fascinating aspects to watch. The addition of Jaylen Waddle no doubt improves the offense. He makes the receiving room better. He makes Nix better. But he should also help Engram. Having a dynamic receiver like Waddle opens the field for Engram, so it’ll be interesting to see how new offensive coordinator Davis Webb plays off that. Engram brings an element at tight end that benefits Nix and the offense. It’s why Denver signed Engram. So use him. If Engram’s usage increases, it’s another element that defenses have to prepare for. Coupled with the expectation that the Broncos running game is more consistent and improves, Engram is another piece at Webb’s disposal. How this plays out, and the type of role Engram has in Denver’s offense, is something to watch. Getting more of a Joker than “meh” will make the Broncos offense and team better.

title: Discussion: How many Detroit Lions rookies will start by the end of 2026?
summary: Ever since the Detroit Lions have been ran by general manager Brad Holmes, they have valued getting rookie contributors. This has usually meant first-round starters, as expected, but the Lions have also turned later picks into instant impact players. Amon-Ra St. Brown (fourth round, 2021), Kerby Joseph (third round, 2022), Sam LaPorta and Brian Branch […]
full_text: Ever since the Detroit Lions have been ran by general manager Brad Holmes, they have valued getting rookie contributors. This has usually meant first-round starters, as expected, but the Lions have also turned later picks into instant impact players. Amon-Ra St. Brown (fourth round, 2021), Kerby Joseph (third round, 2022), Sam LaPorta and Brian Branch (second round, 2023), and Tate Ratledge (second round, 2025) are just some of the non-firsts that have made a mark as rookies. Some of the rookie listed above did not start from the onset, but by the time the season came to an end, they were entrenched as important parts of the team. Could we see a similar feat for the Lions’ 2026 draft class? Today’s Question of the Day is: How many Lions rookies will be starters by the end of 2026? My answer: Two, Blake Miller and Keith Abney. Miller is an obvious choice, as the first-round pick is the heavy favorite to start at right tackle as early as Week 1. That being said, Larry Borom is still in contention and if he outperforms Miller in training camp and preseason, he could win a starting role—a spot has to be earned, not given. My other choice of Abney is more about opportunity. He was the fourth Lion selected in the draft, but as a cornerback with potential to play inside and outside, there is ample opportunity for him to win a starting spot. With the release of Terrion Arnold, the depth chart ahead of Abney is D.J. Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Ennis Rakestraw, and Roger McCreary. Reed will undoubtedly start if healthy, but none of Ya-Sin, Rakestraw, or McCreary are guaranteed starters. Ya-Sin was solid in relief for the Lions last season, but it is worth remembering that he has not been a full-time starter since 2022. Asking the veteran to play at a career-best level across an entire season might be an unrealistic expectation for the 30-year-old. Unlike Ya-Sin, Rakestraw has age on his side, but he has now battled two significant injuries over his first two seasons and has essentially zero experience on defense. As a former second-round pick, he has the talent to earn a starting role, but he has not earned our benefit of the doubt. As for McCreary, he seems like the sure-fire starter at nickel, but there is an important rule to remember: follow the money. The Lions signed McCreary to a one-year contract worth just $1.2 million. While this was perceived as a steal for the Lions, it also highlights that the team might not view him as a starter—in contrast, the Lions signed Borom to a one-year, $5 million deal as offensive tackle insurance. Abney has a lot of players to challenge for a starting role, but he has as good of a chance to impress as they do. Regarding the other draft selections, the late-round picks of Skyler Gill-Howard and Tyre West are fighting for a roster spot, let alone a starting spot. Of the two players selected ahead of Abney, I think Derrick Moore has the best chance to become a starter by season’s end, but I also think he may fall victim of the Lions lack of defined “starters” on defense. I expect this team to run a rotation along the defensive line, so while Moore might play a decent number of snaps, he might not start ahead of, say, DJ Wonnum. Jimmy Rolder, meanwhile, not only has to usurp Malcolm Rodriguez as the third linebacker, but he would need to justify being the third linebacker on the field in the first place . How many rookies will enter the starting lineup by the end of the season? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Discussion: What defines a ‘successful’ 2026 Detroit Lions season?
summary: “Super Bowl or bust.” It’s a phrase that just about every NFL team adopts every season. Anything short of that is considered a failure by most team standards. At least, that’s the line they have to repeat publicly; otherwise, it looks like the team isn’t giving it their all each year. However, that bar isn’t […]
full_text: Detroit Lions chief operating officer Mike Disner, general manager Brad Holmes and coach Dan Campbell watch drills during rookie minicamp Saturday, May 13, 2023 in Allen Park. “Super Bowl or bust.” It’s a phrase that just about every NFL team adopts every season. Anything short of that is considered a failure by most team standards. At least, that’s the line they have to repeat publicly; otherwise, it looks like the team isn’t giving it their all each year. However, that bar isn’t always realistic for each team. Beyond that, if an organization just shows year-to-year growth, it could be a sign that a championship is coming in the future. The Detroit Lions have been in contention for a title over the past three years and have come up short each time. For many, the only step this team has to make is finally winning a Super Bowl, and anything less than that is a failure. But others may be just hoping for some serious progress from a disappointing 9-8 season last year. So today’s Question of the Day is: What defines a “successful” season for the 2026 Detroit Lions? My answer: At the very least, the Lions need to win the NFC North and win a playoff game. Obviously, I’m just as hungry as everyone else for a Lions championship. And I’d even take a Super Bowl appearance at this point. And to be honest, I do think it’s entirely possible for this team to make a championship run. But as a fan, I do not adhere to “Super Bowl or bust.” If you do, I certainly get it. We’ve waited long enough. It’s a stain on this franchise that they haven’t even made it to The Big Game. However, I’m just looking for a deeply competitive season in which the Lions deliver a respectable performance. Winning this division would be a big triumph given how competitive it is supposed to be. Additionally, it would be nice to shut up Bears fans who believe this division is theirs for the next generation. Oh, and keeping the Packers division title-less for five straight years would be their longest drought since 1994. I like that. But the 2024 season is a stark reminder that a division title and a 15-2 record isn’t satisfying without at least a playoff win. So if Detroit can win a division title and tally another postseason win, that would satisfy me as a successful season and an important step in the right direction. Admittedly, that’s a bit of a low bar, and I may not actually be satisfied unless they at least make the NFC Championship Game, but it’s also important to remember where this team came from. We begged for decades to just make the playoffs here and there. Sure, the bar has been raised by this organization, but I also don’t want to become jaded and lose an appreciation for a competitive, entertaining team—even if they fail to win a championship. What does a successful 2026 Lions season look like to you? Share your thoughts in the comment section.

title: Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview: Will Blake Miller win the starting RT job?
summary: In this installment of our Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview series, we examine the Lions’ offensive tackle room, speculate on current and future roles, and discuss how many players from this group could make the 53-man roster. Previous training camp previews: Roster construction Under the Brad Holmes and Dan Campbell regime, the Lions have consistently added offensive […]
full_text: Detroit Lions offensive tackle Blake Miller speaks to media members during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, May 29, 2026. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images In this installment of our Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview series, we examine the Lions’ offensive tackle room, speculate on current and future roles, and discuss how many players from this group could make the 53-man roster. Previous training camp previews: Quarterback: Can Luke Altmyer force a QB3 role? Running back: How RB roles could shift in 2026 Wide receiver: WR depth roles up for grabs Tight end: How many TEs will make the roster? Roster construction Under the Brad Holmes and Dan Campbell regime, the Lions have consistently added offensive linemen as the season progresses. While they typically begin each season with eight to 10 offensive linemen, they’ve consistently finished with 10 or 11 on the active roster. Let’s take a look at what they’ve done at offensive tackle in the previous five seasons: 2021 : Opened with three offensive tackles (Penei Sewell, Taylor Decker, and Matt Nelson), but finished with four (Will Holden). 2022 : Opened with three OTs (Sewell, Decker, and Nelson), and finished with four (Dan Skipper). 2023 : Opened with three OTs (Sewell, Decker, and Nelson), and finished with four (Skipper). 2024 : Opened and finished with four OTs (Sewell, Decker, Skipper, and Giovanni Manu). 2025 : Opened and finished with three OTs (Sewell, Decker, and Manu; Manu was placed on IR in Week 5 and replaced by Skipper). An offseason of change After five seasons of having Sewell and Decker bookending the offensive line, the Lions released Decker after a complicated early portion of the offseason. Adding to the turnover at offensive tackle, Dan Skipper—who had been OT3 or OT4 over the last four seasons—retired and joined the Lions coaching staff as an offensive assistant. As a result of these offseason moves, the Lions made three major decisions. First, they decided to move Sewell to left tackle—where he played full time in college and sporadically in the NFL—then they quickly signed Michigan native and NFL veteran Larry Borom on the opening day of free agency, and the final big move was selecting Clemson right tackle Blake Miller with pick No. 17 in the first round of the NFL Draft . Additionally, the Lions are expected to get Giovanni Manu back on the field during training camp after an early-season injury sidelined him for the majority of 2025, and they re-signed practice squader Devin Cochran. The battleground Will Blake Miller win the starting RT job? The Lions have said they will let Miller and Borom battle it out for the starting right tackle position, and during spring practices they held true to their word, rotating each player through the first and second team. The Lions aren’t afraid to start a rookie if he earns the job, and historically, this regime’s first-round picks tend to start from the jump. Miller is loaded with more experience than the average rookie, having started 54 games in college, as well as possessing an ideal combination of height (6-foot-7), length (34.25-inch arm length), strength (32 reps on bench press), and athleticism ( RAS: 9.9 ). He was widely considered the most NFL-ready tackle in this draft class. While Miller and Borom will indeed battle it out for the starting right tackle position in training camp, reading between the lines at spring practices gives a strong indication that the Lions are expecting Miller to win the job; Miller took every spring practice rep at right tackle, while Borom split his time between the right and left sides—a more typical cross-training style that you see with a swing OT3. What will Borom’s role be? Borom has a solid history of playing right tackle in the NFL, but he also has starting experience at left tackle and guard. While he’ll get a chance to compete, it appears likely that he is headed for a swing OT3 role, as well as a potential OL6 role in jumbo sets. If Borom can continue his play from the second half of last season (in Miami), he should be considered an upgrade to the Lions OT3 position. His ability to play on both sides of the line, as well as guard in a pinch, gives the Lions a lot of flexibility. He’s also likely to assume the Lions OL6 position, where he’ll “report” as an eligible offensive lineman that lines up in an inline tight end role when the Lions want to add more blocking bulk and power. Is this a make-or-break training camp for Giovanni Manu? After an unmemorable rookie season, followed by a sophomore campaign that saw him initially win the OT3 role out of training camp, only to land on injured reserve after four games and never return, Manu could be entering a make-or-break training camp in 2025. The section on roster construction tells the story here. In 2025, Manu was the third and final tackle on the roster for the first month of the season. In 2024, the Lions kept four tackles, but only kept three active on game day, with Manu acting as a weekly healthy scratch. In the previous three seasons, only three offensive tackles made the initial roster under this regime. With Sewell, Miller, and Borom looking solid in roles, Manu will either need to make significant improvement in his development to challenge for the OT3 role, or show enough promise that he forces the Lions to break from their typical roster construction plans and keep an OT4. That’s a tough road. Cross-training OTs One of the reasons the Lions have previously kept only three offensive tackles on the active roster is that they typically stash at least one pure tackle on the practice squad and cross-train some of their interior depth for emergencies. Colby Sorsdal, Miles Frazier, Mason Miller, and rookie Melvin Priestly all have extensive experience playing tackle in college and have previously, or are expected to, cross-train inside-and-out this training camp. Sorsdal began his NFL career repping at right tackle, then kicked inside and cross-trained the previous two seasons. This spring, during OTAs and minicamp, Sorsdal was back at right tackle opposite Cochran on the third-team. Unless he can climb the depth chart in camp, Sorsdal will likely be positioning himself for a spot on the practice squad. Frazier spent a season as LSU’s left tackle, but he has twice as much experience at guard, and it shouldn’t be surprising that he’s been mainly repping inside in Detroit. That being said, coach Dan Campbell has repeatedly said Frazier is being cross-trained at tackle for emergencies, and when you combine that with his overall upside—he’s expected to, at a minimum, win a reserve job on the active roster—his development could be yet another obstacle for Manu to overcome.

title: Ranking every 2026 Detroit Lions player: 30-21 — The new, key depth
summary: The countdown of the Detroit Lions’ 2026 roster continues with players our staff ranked from 30 to 21. These players represent the essential depth on the team. Almost all 10 of these players are expected to play some sort of significant role, be it on special teams, subpackages, or the primary backup plan in case […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - NOVEMBER 16: Detroit Lions linebacker Derrick Barnes (55) reacts in the first half during the game between the Detroit Lions and Philadelphia Eagles on November 16, 2025 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Kyle Ross/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The countdown of the Detroit Lions’ 2026 roster continues with players our staff ranked from 30 to 21. These players represent the essential depth on the team. Almost all 10 of these players are expected to play some sort of significant role, be it on special teams, subpackages, or the primary backup plan in case of injury—there are even some starters in here. What I found particularly interesting about this portion of the list is that half of the players are newcomers. Detroit is going to rely on a lot of new faces to be their primary depth, and their performances could be the difference between the season being a success or failure. Here are the players we ranked from 30 to 21. Previously: Players ranked 90-81 Players ranked 80-71 Players ranked 70-61 Players ranked 60-51 Players ranked 50-41 Players ranked 40-31 30. OT Larry Borom (Highest: 29 Lowest: 41) Last year’s ranking: N/A The Lions really hyped up the addition of Borom in free agency as a real candidate to start at right tackle after a strong finish to last season with the Dolphins. Whether that was genuine or an effort to mask their draft intentions is unclear, but the addition of Blake Miller likely puts Borom as OT3 rather than as a starter. Still, it’s a significant upgrade over Dan Skipper. 29. CB Ennis Rakestraw (Highest 26; Lowest: 37) Last year’s ranking: 33 It’s interesting to see Rakestraw climb in the rankings despite missing all of 2025 with an injury. Is this a sign of worse depth on the team, or did the staff simply rank him higher because expectations are higher for Rakestraw? The third-year corner has barely played in his young NFL career, but with Terrion Arnold now gone, Rakestraw is expected to compete for a starting job. 28. LB Malcolm Rodriguez (Highest: 25; Lowest: 32) Last year’s ranking: 32 It’s the same kind of story with Rodriguez. He missed most of 2025 due to his recovery from a torn ACL, and when he returned to the field, he didn’t look like himself. Now he climbs four spots, likely because the expectations are for him to be LB3 after the departure of Alex Anzalone in free agency. Rodriguez still has to prove he can be a starting linebacker in this league, so his 2026 season will be critical. 27. RB Isiah Pacheco (Highest: 18; Lowest: 48) Last year’s ranking: N/A For comparison’s sake, David Montgomery came in at 11th on last year’s list , so it’s clear our staff believes Pacheco is a significant downgrade, particularly with his recent struggles with injury. However, Pacheco is still just 27 years old, and he’s only a couple years removed from a season in which he put up 935 rushing yards and seven touchdowns. If he can recapture even a fraction of that player, Detroit will have found a great, affordable replacement for D-Mo. 26. P Jack Fox (Highest: 18; Lowest: 48) Last year’s ranking: 26 No one on this year’s countdown had a larger disparity in votes than Fox. He’s typically pretty polarizing in these polls because it’s hard to know where to put an All-Pro-level punter. On one hand, he’s, well, a punter. On the other hand, he’s arguably one of the Lions’ best players at his given position. And he’s coming off a year in which he put a career-high 28 punts inside the 20-yard line with only two touchbacks (career-low). Despite the large disparity in votes, he rather miraculously lands at the same ranking as last year. 25. S Christian Izien (Highest: 21; Lowest: 32) Last year’s ranking: N/A Izien is part of the cavalcade of safeties Detroit signed and re-signed to help navigate the tough injury situations surrounding Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph. Unlike Chuck Clark (44 on our countdown), Izien brings youth (26 years old) and serious long-term potential to the position. Despite entering the league as an undrafted prospect, Izien has already made 45 game appearances and 15 starts in three years. Now, he’ll have a chance to take the next step in his career by competing for a starting job. 24. EDGE Derrick Moore (Highest: 20; Lowest 33) Last year’s rankings: N/A Like any rookie, it’s hard to know what to expect from second-round pick Derrick Moore. With the addition of DJ Wonnum, the Lions won’t overload Moore, but if the former Wolverine can impress early, it’s possible he has a massive role in Detroit’s pass rush this upcoming season. He’s coming off a 10.0 sack season in Ann Arbor, and with a decent supporting cast around him, he’s entering a fairly favorable situation. 23. DT Levi Onwuzurike (Highest: 14; Lowest: 31) Last year’s rankings: 20 Expectations were high for Onwuzurike last year before Lions fans were blindsided with the news that his entire season would be lost to an ACL injury. This year feels like the last chance for Detroit’s former second-round pick, but it’s hard not to get excited about how he looked during his last fully healthy season. He produced 47 pressures in 2024, including seven games in which he had at least four (per PFF). With the back and ACL injuries firmly in the rear-view mirror, is it finally time for Onwuzurike to live up to his potential? 22. LB Derrick Barnes (Highest: 21; Lowest: 25) Last year’s rankings: 19 Barnes falls out of the top-20 after a disappointing 2025 season. But in 2026, the Lions need him more than ever. He will almost certainly take over many of the roles Anzalone had last year, in addition to bringing the SAM linebacker skillset Detroit valued when giving him the 2025 extension. In my opinion, Barnes is one of the most important Lions of the 2026 season, but he’s also one of the bigger mysteries. 21. CB Roger McCreary (Highest: 16; Lowest: 29) Last year’s rankings: N/A McCreary is also a critically important player for the Lions this year after Arnold’s departure. Capable of playing both the slot and outside, Detroit mainly deployed him at nickel in the spring. But that could change now, and McCreary played quite well for the Rams at outside corner during the playoff run last year. Regardless of where he plays, the expectation is for McCreary to play a significant amount of ball for Detroit, and the Lions are hoping the 2022 second-round pick offers an improvement from Amik Robertson’s 2025 season.

title: What are the Colts’ most valuable trade assets? Ranking Nos. 5-1
summary: After looking at players No. 10 through No. 6 in the Colts’ trade-value rankings, the second part of this exercise turns to the team’s most valuable assets. This does not mean Indianapolis should trade any of these players, and in most cases, the Colts would be creating a major roster hole by even considering it. […]
full_text: After looking at players No. 10 through No. 6 in the Colts’ trade-value rankings , the second part of this exercise turns to the team’s most valuable assets. This does not mean Indianapolis should trade any of these players, and in most cases, the Colts would be creating a major roster hole by even considering it. The goal is simply to estimate each player’s league-wide trade value based on age, production, contract, position and how valuable similar players tend to be around the NFL. 5. Laiatu Latu Projected trade value: Second-round pick, possibly a late first Latu’s value is built on age, contract control and positional importance. Young edge rushers with legitimate pass-rush upside are among the most valuable players in football, and Latu has already shown enough to be viewed as a building block for the Colts’ defense. He is not just a rotational player anymore. He is someone teams would look at and believe there is still another level coming. A second-round pick feels like the safest projected value, but there is a real argument that the number could climb higher. If a team believed Latu was on the verge of becoming a double-digit sack edge rusher, a late first-round pick would not be impossible. Edge is too important, and young pass rushers do not become available often. For the Colts, trading him would make very little sense. They need more pass rush, not less, and moving Latu would create the same type of hole they have been trying to fill for years. Still, in a pure trade-value exercise, he belongs this high because of the position he plays and the trajectory he appears to be on. 4. Quenton Nelson Projected trade value: Second-round pick plus a Day 3 pick Nelson is still one of the best guards in football, and his league-wide reputation remains extremely strong. He is consistent, durable, powerful and respected around the NFL. The reason his value is not higher comes down to age, contract and position. Guards are valuable, but they do not carry the same trade market as quarterbacks, left tackles, edge rushers or corners. Nelson’s salary would also factor into the return, which probably keeps him out of first-round territory. A second-round pick plus a Day 3 selection feels realistic. A contender with offensive line issues could justify that kind of move, especially if it believed Nelson was the difference between a good line and a dominant one. For the Colts, though, Nelson is still worth more than the pick package because of what he means to the offensive identity and the stability he gives the line. 3. Jonathan Taylor Projected trade value: Second-round pick or third-round pick plus another selection Taylor is still one of the best running backs in football, but running back trade value is always complicated. His talent says he should be worth a premium pick. The market for veteran running backs says teams would be more cautious. That is why his projected value probably sits somewhere between a straight second-round pick and a third-round pick plus another selection. A contender with a strong roster and a clear need at running back could talk itself into paying the higher price, especially because Taylor can still change an offense when healthy. He is not just a volume back. He is a game-breaking player who can carry a team through stretches and force defenses to adjust. The issue is that teams are careful with age, mileage and contract cost at the position. Taylor’s value to the Colts is likely higher than his value on the open market because he is still the centerpiece of their offense. Trading him would remove the one player who can consistently tilt the field for Indianapolis, and unless the return was overwhelming, it would be hard to justify. 2. Tyler Warren Projected trade value: Late first-round pick or early second-round pick plus more Warren is the most interesting player on the list because his value is based on youth, upside and cheap contract control. If a young tight end looks like a future difference-maker, the trade value becomes significant quickly. He gives the Colts a rare offensive piece: a player who can win as a receiver, create mismatches, help the run game and become a long-term security blanket for the quarterback. The positional value of tight end keeps this from being a clean top-of-the-first-round type return, but a late first-round pick feels reasonable if another team believes he is on the path to becoming a top-tier player at the position. At minimum, an early second-round pick plus another selection would have to be the conversation. For Indianapolis, Warren is exactly the kind of player a team should want to keep. Young, talented offensive weapons on rookie contracts are extremely valuable, and his role should only grow. This is one of those cases where the trade value may be high, but the practical answer is simple: the Colts should not be interested unless a team badly overpays. 1. Sauce Gardner Projected trade value: Two first-round picks Gardner is the easiest name on the list. The Colts already know his value because they paid a massive price to get him. Elite cornerbacks in their prime do not come cheap, and Gardner checks every major box: age, talent, reputation, position value and proven production. He is one of the rare defensive backs who can change the way a defense is built because he gives a team a true No. 1 corner. Two first-round picks is the right projected value because that is the level of player he is. If anything, the Colts would probably need more than that to seriously consider moving him, especially after already making the aggressive decision to acquire him. Trading him away would defeat the entire purpose of the move. Gardner is the most valuable trade asset on the roster because he combines premium-position value with rare talent and prime years still ahead of him. The Colts have good players, but he is the one whose trade market would be the strongest, cleanest and easiest to define. Final thought The top of the Colts’ trade-value list shows where the roster has legitimate high-end pieces. Gardner is the clear No. 1, Warren is the young offensive asset with the most upside, and Taylor, Nelson, Latu and Raimann all carry strong value for different reasons. That does not mean Indianapolis should move any of them. In most cases, the player is more useful to the Colts than the draft pick would be. This exercise is more about understanding how the league would likely view the roster, and the answer is clear: the Colts have several players with meaningful trade value, but only Gardner sits in the true blockbuster category.

title: Ranking the Colts’ most valuable trade assets: Nos. 10-6
summary: Before getting into the list, it is important to make the purpose clear. This does not mean the Colts should trade any of these players, and it does not mean they would accept these offers if another team called. Some players are worth more to Indianapolis than they would be on the open market, and […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - JUNE 11: Indianapolis Colts safety Cam Bynum (0) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts Minicamp on June 11, 2026 at the Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Before getting into the list, it is important to make the purpose clear. This does not mean the Colts should trade any of these players, and it does not mean they would accept these offers if another team called. Some players are worth more to Indianapolis than they would be on the open market, and in other cases, the hole created by trading the player would be bigger than the draft pick coming back. This is simply an attempt to assign league-wide trade value based on age, talent, contract, position, production, scarcity and how NFL teams usually value similar players. The 2026 draft class was not included in the list. 10. Charvarius Ward Projected trade value: Fourth-round pick Ward still has value because quality outside corners are hard to find, and teams are always looking for veteran defensive backs who can step into a starting role. He has played high-level football, has the reputation of a reliable cover corner, and would make sense for a contender that needs help on the outside. The reason his value settles around a fourth-round pick is age and contract. Ward is a good player, but he is not the kind of young, ascending corner who would command a premium return. For the Colts, he may be more useful on the roster than he would be as a trade asset because Indianapolis needs proven cornerback depth around Sauce Gardner. Still, if a team were desperate for a starting-caliber veteran corner, a fourth-round pick feels like the realistic range. 9. Cam Bynum Projected trade value: Fourth-round pick, possibly a third Bynum is a good player, and he gives the Colts stability at safety, which is something they badly needed. He is smart, reliable, versatile and experienced enough to help organize the back end of the defense. Those traits have value, especially for teams looking for a steady safety rather than a boom-or-bust athlete. The issue is positional value. Safeties rarely bring back major trade returns unless they are elite, extremely young, or on a bargain contract. Bynum is valuable, but he is probably more valuable to the Colts than he would be to another team in a trade. A fourth-round pick feels like the safest estimate, although a desperate contender could talk itself into a third if it viewed him as the missing piece in the secondary. 8. Daniel Jones Projected trade value: Conditional third-round pick Jones is the hardest player in this range to evaluate because his value depends almost entirely on how he plays this season. If he stabilizes the Colts’ offense, protects the football, and looks like a legitimate starting quarterback again, a conditional third-round pick would be very reasonable. Starting quarterbacks, even imperfect ones, have value because there are never enough of them. If he plays like a bridge quarterback, the value drops quickly. That is why a conditional pick makes the most sense. A team trading for Jones would likely want protection based on starts, performance, or playoff results. The upside case is that he becomes a useful starter and Indianapolis could get a strong Day 2 return. The downside is that the league still views him as a temporary option, which would push his value much closer to Day 3. 7. Alec Pierce Projected trade value: Third-round pick, possibly a second Pierce is a tricky one because his value depends on how the league views his skill set. If a team sees him as a high-end vertical threat who can be a strong No. 2 receiver, then a second-round pick is not impossible. Size, speed and downfield production still matter, and Pierce can change the structure of a defense when he is winning deep. The more realistic range is probably a third-round pick, though. Wide receiver is a deep position around the league, and teams may hesitate to give up a premium pick for a player they view as more specialized than complete. For the Colts, Pierce has more value because he fits a specific role in their offense and gives them a vertical element they do not easily replace. On the trade market, his best return would likely come from a contender that needs a field-stretcher and believes it can unlock even more from him. 6. Bernhard Raimann Projected trade value: Second-round pick Raimann may be one of the most underrated trade assets on the roster. Quality starting left tackles are extremely valuable, and Raimann has developed into a reliable player at one of the most important positions in football. Teams do not usually find starting-caliber left tackles easily, which is why his trade value should be strong. A second-round pick feels like the floor if the Colts ever made him available. Depending on contract status and how another team grades him, he could even push closer to a late first-round conversation. The reason he is not higher on this list is that he does not have the same league-wide name value as some of the Colts’ bigger stars, but in terms of actual roster-building value, Raimann is one of the most important players Indianapolis has. Trading him would create a major hole, which is why this is more of a value exercise than something the Colts should seriously consider.
