title: Jaguars draft class: 5 things to know about Zach Durfee
summary: Zach Durfee may have arrived in Jacksonville as a seventh-round pick, but his path to the NFL is anything but ordinary. From walking away from football to becoming an anonymous ESPN sensation, here are five things you probably didn’t know about one of the Jaguars‘ most intriguing developmental prospects. Better at Basketball? Long before NFL […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - MAY 09: Zach Durfee #58 of the Jacksonville Jaguars goes through workout drills during Rookie Mini Camp at Miller Electric Center on May 9, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images) | Getty Images Zach Durfee may have arrived in Jacksonville as a seventh-round pick, but his path to the NFL is anything but ordinary. From walking away from football to becoming an anonymous ESPN sensation, here are five things you probably didn’t know about one of the Jaguars ‘ most intriguing developmental prospects. Better at Basketball? We have selected Washington DE Zach Durfee with the No. 233 overall pick! @Dream_Finders | #NFLDraft pic.twitter.com/DTzY27AFeT — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) April 25, 2026 Long before NFL scouts were discussing Zach Durfee’s pass-rushing potential, many believed his future lay on the basketball court. Growing up in the tiny town of Tyler, Minnesota, Durfee excelled in multiple sports, but basketball was arguably where he shone brightest. Standing well over six feet tall with impressive athleticism, he averaged more than 20 points and 10 rebounds per game during his senior season, earning all-state recognition and attracting genuine collegiate interest. Football, meanwhile, was almost a side project. He played quarterback, receiver and defensive end for Dawson-Boyd High School, but unlike many future NFL players, he wasn’t immersed in elite camps or travelling across the country for recruiting showcases. Instead, he developed as a well-rounded athlete in a rural community where playing multiple sports was the norm rather than the exception. That background may have helped shape the player Jacksonville eventually drafted. Basketball develops footwork, balance and lateral quickness—traits that translate remarkably well to rushing the passer. Watch Durfee explode off the edge or change direction in pursuit, and it’s easy to spot the influence of years spent defending guards and attacking the basket. It’s a reminder that some NFL careers don’t begin with endless football training. Sometimes they start in a small-town gymnasium, chasing rebounds rather than quarterbacks. The Late Starter Remember Zach Durfee ( @zach_durfee ) from the University of Sioux Falls? He's now a Washington Husky and had THREE sacks this past Saturday pic.twitter.com/KIGSIZwqKA — Tanner Castora (@Tanner_Castora) September 13, 2024 Durfee’s journey to the NFL is unusual because, for a while, it looked like there wouldn’t be one at all. After graduating from high school, he enrolled at North Dakota State—a powerhouse of FCS football that has produced stars including Carson Wentz and Christian Watson. Yet Durfee wasn’t part of that programme. Instead, he attended as a regular student and stepped away from competitive football altogether. Many players lose interest during that period and never return. Durfee did the opposite. Eventually transferring to the University of Sioux Falls, he committed himself fully to football and, crucially, to learning defensive end. Unlike many NFL edge rushers who have spent a decade refining pass-rush moves, Durfee was still discovering the nuances of the position well into his college career. Every season became an opportunity to learn hand placement, leverage, counter moves and the technical details that elite prospects often master years earlier. That makes his rise even more remarkable. Rather than benefiting from years of specialist coaching, he compressed his development into a relatively short period before attracting NFL attention. It’s one of the reasons scouts remain intrigued by his long-term upside. Jacksonville aren’t simply drafting the player Durfee is today—they’re betting on what he could become after receiving full-time professional coaching. One Obstacle After Another #Jaguars rookie EDGE Zach Durfee at OTAs pic.twitter.com/gx8lMazn31 — Gus Logue (@gus_logue) May 26, 2026 Momentum and misfortune seemed to arrive hand in hand throughout Durfee’s college career. After bursting onto the scene at Sioux Falls, he earned an opportunity to transfer to Washington, giving him the chance to prove himself against Power Four competition. It should have been the breakthrough he’d worked towards for years. Instead, setbacks followed almost immediately. Transfer eligibility rules limited his opportunities, while injuries repeatedly interrupted his progress. An elbow problem sidelined him, only for turf toe—a notoriously frustrating injury for explosive athletes—to strike later. Just as he began building momentum again, further physical issues arrived to halt it once more. For many players, that sequence would have been enough to derail an NFL dream. Instead, Durfee continued earning respect inside Washington’s program. Coaches and teammates consistently praised his work ethic and professionalism, eventually voting him as one of the Huskies’ team captains despite his interrupted playing career. That recognition arguably says more about his character than any sack total ever could. NFL evaluators often talk about resilience being difficult to measure. Durfee’s college career provided plenty of evidence. Every time circumstances knocked him backwards, he found a way to return, earning an NFL opportunity through perseverance as much as production. Think he has a shot to make a roster as a late-round pick or UDFA. https://t.co/CR0UOslWSz pic.twitter.com/cXn4zrxuWW — Devin Jackson (@RealD_Jackson) April 22, 2026 Few seventh-round picks have entered the NFL with quite as much mystery surrounding them. In the build-up to the 2026 NFL Draft, ESPN released one of its annual anonymous prospect features, profiling a player simply known as “Prospect X.” The article detailed an unconventional football journey, multiple injuries, personal adversity and a determination to reach the NFL despite repeated setbacks. Fans immediately began playing detective. Across social media, particularly among Washington supporters, readers dissected every clue. They examined references to a basketball background, small-town upbringing, injuries, relationships and even favourite local restaurants, slowly narrowing the possibilities before concluding that the mystery player had to be Zach Durfee. The speculation generated far more attention than most late-round prospects ever receive. Instead of quietly preparing for the draft, Durfee became the subject of an online guessing game involving thousands of college football fans. When his identity was eventually confirmed, many people who had never watched him play suddenly knew his story. It’s a fitting reflection of Durfee’s football career. He’s rarely taken the conventional path, and even his introduction to the wider football world came wrapped in secrecy rather than headlines. For a player selected late on Day Three, that’s a remarkably unique way to arrive in the NFL. Hidden Freak Zach Durfee is a DE prospect in the 2026 draft class. He scored a 9.77 RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 50 out of 2094 DE from 1987 to 2026. https://t.co/NpXZreGVlI pic.twitter.com/Wn1EkoUvCD — RAS.football (@MathBomb) March 21, 2026 On paper, seventh-round draft picks rarely possess elite athletic traits. Durfee is the exception. Despite slipping to the latter stages of the draft, his testing numbers placed him among the more explosive edge defenders available. At around 6-foot-5 and more than 250 pounds, he reportedly ran in the mid-4.5s over 40 yards while posting a vertical jump approaching 39 inches. Those are eye-catching figures for any pass rusher and help explain why scouts remained intrigued despite his limited résumé. The biggest question was never his physical ability. In 2002, he set the team’s single-season tackle record (162) at the time in his only year as a full-season starter. title: Put on a show, Ty Simpson
summary: Training camp kicks off this week for the Los Angeles Rams. Matthew Stafford returns from his 2025 MVP campaign. High-profile additions like Trent McDuffie, Myles Garrett, and Jaylen Watson will make their debuts. Aaron Donald could un-retire soon. There’s plenty of exciting news surrounding the Rams. No story may be bigger over training camp and […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - APRIL 23: Alabama quarterback Ty Simpson reacts as he puts on a hat after being chosen 13th overall by the Los Angeles Rams in the tunnel during the the first round NFL football draft at Acrisure Stadium on April 23, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp kicks off this week for the Los Angeles Rams. Matthew Stafford returns from his 2025 MVP campaign. High-profile additions like Trent McDuffie, Myles Garrett, and Jaylen Watson will make their debuts. Aaron Donald could un-retire soon. There’s plenty of exciting news surrounding the Rams. No story may be bigger over training camp and the preseason than rookie quarterback and 2026 first-round pick Ty Simpson. LA’s selection of Simpson sent shockwaves across the NFL world. Instead of drafting another playmaker to get the most out of Stafford’s remaining tenure, the Rams instead opted to prepare for life after their franchise quarterback. Simpson is going to dominate headlines. The vibe will shift on every positive or negative report from practice. We may even get to see him in the preseason, and it’s all but certain that people will drop sweeping conclusions from a very limited sample size. Rams fans haven’t seen a show like this since Jared Goff was picked first overall pack in 2016. They aren’t used to young quarterback news cycles and the drama that surrounds them. It is imperative to stay even keeled. Simpson is the future of the team. It will take time for him to develop. This has always been the Rams’ plan and they have the rare luxury of patience. So let’s get out in front of the wave and set realistic expectations. Put on a show, Ty Simpson Training camp is not a relevant measuring stick for the likes of Garrett, McDuffie, Watson, or Donald. Their real test will come in Week 1 when the Rams travel to Australia to take on the San Francisco 49ers. But camp is effectively Simpson’s Super Bowl. He may not even play in the preseason. So before the rookie gets put on mothballs, why not put on a show and demonstrate why the Rams felt confident selecting him at thirteenth overall? If all goes according to plan, training camp and preseason are our only opportunities to check in on Simpson’s development. Then time will freeze and we will hold all prior conclusions until this time next year, of which Simpson should either enter as the presumed starter or in store for another year as Stafford’s understudy. Simpson’s debut can be spectacularly awful or promising. It doesn’t matter or have any impact on the outlook of his NFL career. He just needs to let loose and show a few glimpses of what the Rams saw ahead of the draft. Is the backup QB battle ‘rigged’? I view the backup job behind Stafford as entirely Stetson Bennett’s to lose. Third quarterbacks are effectively inactive on gamedays unless the top two are injured. That means if something happens to the starter, the backup is going to play. There is no alternative realistically. That is exactly the reason why Simpson should not enter the regular season as Stafford’s backup. He shouldn’t play until Sean McVay believes he is ready and applies his metaphorical stamp of approval. Could Simpson be ready before Week 1? I guess it’s possible. I’m more inclined to believe that Simpson will need time and the transition could happen at the earliest somewhere around the season’s midpoint. So in short, don’t panic when Simpson loses the quarterback battle. Bennett could easily win the job but not truly be the better of the two players. The Rams have a difficult decision to make in terms of balancing the short-term and long-term interests of the team. Simpson may give the Rams a better chance to win this season. Playing him could skewer the remainder of his career and skew perceptions, similar to what happened to Goff as a rookie. Will we see Simpson in the preseason? McVay and the Rams do not value the preseason. Any player who holds a meaningful role generally sits out. LA should also try to avoid a disastrous JJ McCarthy-type injury with Simpson, as that would significantly hinder his development. But if the backup quarterback battle is truly “rigged”, meaning it’s Bennett’s to lose, then Bennett shouldn’t play in the preseason either. By pure process of elimination, Simpson should play . The real question is if Simpson plays, how much is there to really learn? Teams run vanilla offenses in exhibition games in order to preserve secrecy ahead of the regular season. Simpson likely wouldn’t even be running McVay’s real plays. Defenses also keep schemes, coverages, and blitzes vanilla too. It’s football but not necessarily real football. And if Simpson does play, people will attempt to make up their mind about the trajectory of the quarterback’s career even though (1) we knew he needed time to develop behind the scenes and the Rams are uniquely equipped to afford that opportunity, (2) he’s not running the Rams’ best plays, (3) isn’t playing with a normal supporting cast, and (4) doesn’t have much playing experience under his belt. Patience has always been key for Ty Simpson. Even though we are set to get our first glimpses of his NFL career, fans should also be open minded and patient. Training camp struggles do not indicate that the Rams wasted the thirteenth overall pick or that Simpson will never be a good NFL quarterback. Positive signs should also be taken with a grain of salt. We will overreact because this is our only opportunity to see Simpson until this time next year. We shouldn’t. Just enjoy the show.

title: Rams fans want to hear what Seattle’s Grey Zabel had to say
summary: Seattle Seahawks Super Bowl Champion guard, Grey Zabel, gave some incredibly high praise for Poona Ford, Kobie Turner, and the Los Angeles Rams as a whole. He complimented Ford and Turner as great players, the type of athletes that make Zabel work, and want to play the game of football. He expressed some appreciation towards […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 25: Grey Zabel #76 of the Seattle Seahawks looks on during the first quarter of the NFC Championship game against the Los Angeles Rams at Lumen Field on January 25, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jane Gershovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images Seattle Seahawks Super Bowl Champion guard, Grey Zabel, gave some incredibly high praise for Poona Ford, Kobie Turner, and the Los Angeles Rams as a whole. He complimented Ford and Turner as great players, the type of athletes that make Zabel work, and want to play the game of football. He expressed some appreciation towards the Rams group as a whole for being a bunch of “really good dudes” . Right or wrong, hate can be a part of sports at times, and as much as one loves Ben Jonhson (head coach of the Chicago Bears) hating the Green Bay Packers, it’s also one of the cooler things in pro sports to see players out for blood during a game, but then coming together when the final whistle blows. These guys are family, friends and or peers who tend to, but not always, have a mutual respect for each other. Zabel, in this interview, showed love to the Rams despite knowing that he’ll have to do battle with them again at least twice in the upcoming season. Said Zabel on the Green Light with Chris Long Podcast: “Poona Ford’s a great example. Dude, just pure raw strength. Like, he picked me up, like just lifted me up as I was trying to base block him, and I’m like, ‘Alright, yah I can’t do anything about it’. Kobie Turner’s the same way…I know for a fact that I would ten times out of ten, I would rather block a bigger, stronger, slower guy than some short, stocky, quick dude who can go side-to side in just like, the blink of a second.” Zabel was then asked about, and discussed the moment after the Seahawks’ NFC Championship win over the Rams when Zabel immediately went up to Kobie Turner. Zabel explained that he was bummed Turner got hurt in the game, and he wanted Turner to know how much Zabel values facing off against him. Sean McVay and Les Snead talk about wanting to draft guys who love football and according to Zabel, Turner is exactly that. Also, based on Zabel’s response, he seems to love football as much as anyone else in the league right now. “Well, first off, Kobie Turner is like my kryptonite right now in the game of football. Like, I don’t know what it is, he’s just got my number, he just works me every single game, but it’s so cool. Like I said, as much you, like, want to hate the Rams, like, they’re all really good dudes. Across the board. And like Kobie, for instance, he’s out there and he just smiles. Like he just plays the game for the love of the game. No question about it. And it was a sad deal because he got a little banged up, and he couldn’t finish that NFC Championship Game. So, the moment after the game was done, I just went and talked to him, talked how awesome he was, and what a great game…how fun it is to compete against him. And he’s just an unbelievable guy. I mean, if anybody watching knows Kobie, they know exactly what I’m talking about because it’s…he’s top tier. He’s what makes the game fun to play against defensive lineman.” Whether you win or lose, being a good sport involves showing respect to all involved, and Zabel very much humbled himself by being overtly positive when it came to talking about the Rams. He could have said anything, and he chose to show appreciation to his division rival. Now, if the Rams find a way to beat the Seahawks this year, it will be interesting to see how high Zabel is on the Rams then, but that potential situation won’t come until later this year. For now, it’s peace and love across the NFL in July. Let’s check back in on the Rams and Zabel’s mood after their first matchup in December.

title: All major storylines surrounding Rams as training camp opens
summary: Players report to training camp for the Los Angeles Rams on Saturday, July 25th. LA opens the regular season in Melbourne, Australia against the San Francisco 49ers on Thursday, September 10th. There are several major open questions surrounding the Rams that have lingered from the offseason. Training camp is certain to bring more information and […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - JANUARY 10: Los Angeles Rams offensive tackle Alaric Jackson (77) looks on during the NFC Wildcard playoff game against the Carolina Panthers on January 10, 2026 at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Joe Robbins/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Players report to training camp for the Los Angeles Rams on Saturday, July 25th . LA opens the regular season in Melbourne, Australia against the San Francisco 49ers on Thursday, September 10th. There are several major open questions surrounding the Rams that have lingered from the offseason. Training camp is certain to bring more information and some answers. These are the major storylines as the Rams head to Loyola Marymount University: Potential discipline for Alaric Jackson Jackson will reportedly not face felony criminal charges for his June 8th arrest. But the NFL is generally more strict than the law in order to uphold the image of the shield. Jackson is a repeat offender in the eyes of the league as he served a two-game suspension back in 2024 for a personal conduct violation. The second offense usually carries a baseline six-game suspension, although the NFL will likely conduct an investigation and draw their own conclusions. The Rams don’t have a lot of good options behind Jackson. Veteran tackles David Quessenberry and AJ Arcuri are on the roster. LA drafted Keagen Trost in the third round this spring and he brings a wealth of college experience. The backup plan seems lackluster. The Rams seem to be crossing their fingers for good news on the suspension front. Will Aaron Donald make return official? There is plenty of speculation that Donald could return to the Rams and unite with Myles Garrett . For some, it probably doesn’t feel like much of a question. Donald seems slated to return as long as he feels he’s physically capable of performing at a high level. What is there left to say? We are just waiting until Donald confirms one way or the other. A lot of players need new contracts LA is in a tough spot when it comes to extending star receiver Puka Nacua. Nacua entered rehabilitation earlier this offseason, and for that reason any franchise would be nervous about paying him top dollar. On the other hand, Nacua’s price tag will only increase if he has another productive season. It’s generally smarter money to pay players earlier and beat the rest of the league to contract inflation. Nacua is the biggest domino to fall on the contract front for the Rams. Also worth keeping on the radar are: Steve Avila, LG Kobie Turner, DT Byron Young, EDGE Colby Parkinson, TE Kevin Dotson, RG We know the Rams like to take care of extension around the time training camp kicks off. There is likely to be some news on this front in the coming few weeks, although it may not be for whom you are expecting. Is the offensive personnel shift real? The Rams are signaling that their role of third receiver has been diminished as the team transitions to deployment of more tight ends. But LA has primarily used 11 personnel (three receivers) since Sean McVay took over as head coach in 2017. We’ve heard the talk before. Walking the walk is a different story. Could the 12 and 13 personnel trend go as quickly as it came? The Rams don’t really have the horses to seriously threaten defense in 11 personnel. I’ll wait to believe it until I see it. Also on this topic, training camp will be helpful in validating the potential second-year breakout of TE Terrance Ferguson. Ferguson enters the season as one of the most important offensive chess pieces due to his role as a TE/WR hybrid. He could be the key to unlocking the passing game in heavier personnel sets. Renewing commitment to special teams LA invested in special teams this offseason for the first time in a long while. They signed long snapper Joe Cardona, specialist Grant Stuard, and hired Bubba Ventrone and Kyle Hole as special teams coordinator and assistant, respectively. But one important position the Rams did not address is at return man. Xavier Smith is the leading man for this role until he is usurped, and I’d question how likely that outcome would be. Our last memory of Smith was a muffed punt in the NFC Championship game that gifted the Seahawks a touchdown. LA can do better here and they didn’t seem keen on improving. Will a new tone at the top and veteran leadership make a difference in the third phase? Quarterbacks, quarterbacks, quarterbacks It’s a big story in the NFL when the reigning MVP takes the field for training camp for a new season. Matthew Stafford is certain to get his flowers from the media for his 2026 campaign. It wouldn’t be surprising if coverage of Ty Simpson outshines Stafford in training camp. This is simply because we likely won’t see Simpson in the regular season. Practices and potentially preseason are our only chances to check in on LA’s first-round pick. It’s no secret that Simpson was a controversial selection. If he struggles, the internet and media will be quick to bury him. The rookie will be the talk of training camp. And Simpson is “battling” Stetson Bennett for the backup spot behind Stafford, although I’d suggest this is overblown. The backup role should be Bennett’s to lose. The Rams most independently decide when Simpson is capable of starting, and he should not be thrust into action prematurely. The backup role could comprimise his development.

title: The Rams aren’t alone waiting to sign their quarterback draft pick
summary: Ty Simpson isn’t the only early 2026 draft pick who still hasn’t signed their first contract. In fact, four quarterbacks and seven selections total still haven’t put pen to paper. The first four quarterbacks drafted this year, including Fernando Mendoza (first overall), Simpson (13th), Carson Beck (65th) and Drew Allar (76th) are all without a […]
full_text: WOODLAND HILLS, CALIFORNIA - JUNE 01: Ty Simpson #15 of the Los Angeles Rams drops back to pass during an OTA offseason workout at Rams Village at Warner Center on June 1, 2026 in Woodland Hills, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ty Simpson isn’t the only early 2026 draft pick who still hasn’t signed their first contract. In fact, four quarterbacks and seven selections total still haven’t put pen to paper. The first four quarterbacks drafted this year, including Fernando Mendoza (first overall), Simpson (13th), Carson Beck (65th) and Drew Allar (76th) are all without a deal so far, although it’s still far too early to be genuinely concerned about this. Since the rookie wage scale was implemented in 2011, every draft pick has a specific value each year. In other words, before the draft even starts, the total value of every pick’s contract is already set. Unlike the pre-2011 lockout world, when draft picks could negotiate salaries and early picks would eat up massive amounts of cap space, every team already knows what their picks will make, at least in terms of general value. Matthew Stafford, for example, got a six-year contract with a total value of $72 million when he was drafted by the Detroit Lions in 2009, with $41.7 million guaranteed. The salary cap was also just $123 million in 2009. For an example even closer to home, Sam Bradford’s holdout and subsequent massive contract he signed following the 2010 draft was the final nail in the coffin for the old way of doing things. Needless to say, that’s not what’s happening with Ty Simpson and his fellow top-three round quarterbacks this year. For comparison’s sake, Mendoza’s eventual contract will be fully guaranteed, but will only be worth $57.3 million total value over four years. Simpson’s total value will be right around $25.4 million. In recent years, the hang-ups for draft pick deals have generally involved things like offset language or other relatively minute details. Rookies don’t hold out often anymore, even though there was an example of it last year when Shemar Stewart of the Cincinnati Bengals held out intro training camp. While we don’t have exact details yet, this is likely just the newest relatively minor mutation of the rookie wage scale era. As far as the first-round picks go, Simpson and Mendoza, there hasn’t been much change in how those contracts are done in recent years. The top-overall selection’s contract has been fully guaranteed since the scale was implemented, when Cam Newton signed for $22 million . Both of those aforementioned passers will get fully guaranteed deals this year, too. But the other fine-print details are the likely sticking points, and will likely set a precedent for next year’s class and those beyond it as well. As the #13 overall pick, QB Ty Simpson (Alabama) should sign a fully guaranteed 4-year, $25.4M contract with the #Rams , including a $14.9M signing bonus. Simpson reportedly turned down a $6.5M NIL offer to remain in college football. He'll now earn $15.8M in 2026. He's repped… — Spotrac (@spotrac) April 24, 2026 It’s even easier to guess what’s going on with Beck and Allar, the third and fourth quarterbacks taken in this year’s draft. If you recall last year, almost every second-round pick held out well into July (right around this time last year, right before training camp, fittingly). That was entirely about guaranteed money and how much they were going to get after past second rounders only received partial guarantees on their rookie deals. Now, this year’s 64th-overall pick (Bud Clark for the Seattle Seahawks) has a rookie contract valued at $7.9 million with $5.4 million guaranteed, or, in other words, 68% of the deal is guaranteed. Last year, the 65th pick in the draft, Darius Alexander of the New York Giants, had just under $1.6 million of his $6.7 million overall contract guaranteed, or just below 24%. That’s a sizable disparity. Needless to say, you can understand why a quarterback drafted in that position wants a bigger guarantee. And next year, non-quarterbacks taken in the third round will want a guarantee commensurate with those of their classmates, and the process will continue down the line later and later into the draft. Deadlines spur action, and with training camp looming there’s a soft deadline on the horizon to work these contracts out. At this point it would be shocking if these quarterbacks don’t get on the field soon. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots’ safety room was flipped upside down during Mike Vrabel’s first year as head coach in 2025, as the new coaching staff constructed a fresh foundation. An original duo of Jabrill Peppers and longtime safety Kyle Dugger was reconfigured under Vrabel as Patriots brass looked toward rotational backup Jaylinn Hawkins and fourth-round rookie Craig Woodson to lead the unit. The transition paid off, and now the team will look to build on the group’s success heading into 2026. In the next edition of our Patriots training camp preview series, we’ll take a look at New England’s safety corps in its entirety and discuss the biggest takeaways heading into the summer practices. Veterans will report to the facility on July 24. *Denotes player on the Pats Pulpit 53-man roster projection Depth chart Starters: Kevin Byard (32)* , Craig Woodson (25)* | Backups: Dell Pettus (25)* , Mike Brown (27)* , Brenden Schooler (29)* , John Saunders Jr. (24) , Peter Manuma (23/R) As a mid-round selection, Woodson exceeded expectations last season alongside Hawkins, playing 93.7% of the defensive snaps. But it was during the playoffs that the then-24-year-old made a significant impact during the Patriots’ run through the AFC. Woodson recorded 30 tackles, six pass deflections, one interception and a fumble recovery in those four matchups. Pro Football Focus included the rising safety on its 2025 All-Playoff Team with an 84.3 postseason grade. Despite having a capable duo with Hawkins’ team-leading four interceptions, New England felt it could upgrade by signing 11-year veteran and three-time All-Pro Kevin Byard to a one-year deal . Byard spent six seasons with Vrabel in Tennessee before a two-year stint with the Chicago Bears, helping the franchise to the Divisional Round in 2025. The depth behind the starters consists of Dell Pettus and Mike Brown, who have similar play styles, primarily lining up in the box. Pettus fought his way onto the roster as an undrafted rookie in 2024 and has been a core special-teamer, making appearances in dime packages. Additionally, Brown signed a one-year deal with the Patriots after spending his previous three seasons with the Titans. They are then followed by special teams ace Brenden Schooler, who is used sparingly in specific defensive packages. John Saunders Jr., who was picked up mid-season in 2025 after the team traded Dugger to the Pittsburgh Steelers , was also retained this offseason. Furthermore, an undrafted rookie from Hawaii, Peter Manuma, will provide further competition in training camp. Key question: Who’s the third safety? One of the question marks surrounding this group is the impact its depth will offer next season, and the third safety plays the most important role in that result. Pettus’ defensive snap count regressed by nearly 200 reps last season compared to 2024. Yet, he consistently made reliable plays, most notably breaking up a fourth-down pass attempt against the New York Jets in Week 11 and practically sealing a New England victory. His role on the defense is limited due to his smaller frame, but he’s proven to be a steady rotational player. Brown saw career-high usage in 2024, appearing in all 17 games and registering 49 tackles; however, he was almost strictly a special-teamer last season and only saw action in nine games after ankle and knee injuries. Regardless of that regression in playing time, Brown saw first-team reps in three-safety packages during the spring and could see a larger role with the Patriots. Both safeties seem to have decent shots at making the final roster, so a rotation between the two in those packages is a potential route. X-Factor: Kevin Byard Returning to the top of the depth chart, Byard will be the x-factor of the safety room, manning the deep portions of the field if he continues to defy Father Time. The veteran is turning 33 in August and, in recent years, has grown slightly more inconsistent in man coverage. Still, he’s been playing his role as a roaming safety at an elite level. In 2025, at 32 years old, Byard was the league’s interceptions leader with seven turnovers and, along with eight pass breakups, was elected a First-Team All-Pro. He also proved he remains a physical downfield playmaker, recording 93 tackles and four for a loss. Beyond Byard’s versatility, he extends his influence off the field as a mentor. His playing experience should also aid Woodson’s development as he enters his second season. The duo of Woodson and Byard should create a layer of stability in the shell of the Patriots’ defense next season. Training camp will offer an early indication of where Byard is physically.

title: Sunday Patriots Notes: How A.J. Brown shifts defense’s philosophy
summary: The quiet portion of the NFL offseason is nearly complete as the New England Patriots will soon open training camp. But following the last true week without football, this week’s version of our Sunday Patriots Notes is therefore a shortened one. Naturally, there are always still a few things to talk about. (Photo by Jaiden Tripi/Getty Images) | Getty Images The quiet portion of the NFL offseason is nearly complete as the New England Patriots will soon open training camp. But following the last true week without football, this week’s version of our Sunday Patriots Notes is therefore a shortened one. Naturally, there are always still a few things to talk about. So, let’s dive straight in. Brown effect Kevin Byard was teammates with A.J. Brown for three seasons in Tennessee. He saw first-hand the impact the wide receiver can make. So much, he compared it to that of Justin Jefferson’s in Minnesota, who Byard matched up with four times in his last two seasons in Chicago. “When I was in Chicago, we obviously played against a guy in Justin Jefferson, and, for the most part, you need to point out where Justin Jefferson was on every single play,” Byard said on SiriusXM NFL Radio . “It’s the same thing with A.J. When I’m lined up at safety, and I’m deep back there, 12, 14, 15 yards, whatever, I’m going to identify where’s A.J.? You know what I mean? Like where’s he at? Is he lined up way out on the boundary at the X? Is he lined up in the slot or whatever? “Let’s identify where he is, and now I can kind of get a good base on, OK, this is where the No. 1 player is. The running back’s here; tight end’s here. So, it just shifts your philosophy on how you want to play defense.” Even at age 29, Brown has remained one of the most productive wide receivers in football posting four straight 1,000 yard seasons in Philadelphia. Now in New England, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels is expected to move Brown around to pick mismatches. But, Brown will still do much of his work as a big bodied X receiver on the outside — where he showcased an early impressive connection with Drake Maye in mandatory minicamp. “Do you play cloud over top over top of [Brown]? ‘Cause you don’t really want to leave him one-on-one,” Byard said. “I mean that’s what A.J. does best. He’s going to run those slants, those quick dig routes, those go balls. I don’t think anybody in the league is better than him when it comes to those routes and being able to break a tackle and take it the distance. So, he’s just a phenomenal athlete, phenomenal talent.” Over the offseason break, Brown got together with Drake Maye and other Patriot pass catchers down in North Carolina. As the two continue to build their chemistry, New England hopes Brown’s presence will help Maye lead another top offense in 2026. Roster growth In ESPN’s recent top-10 positional surveys, A.J. Brown was ranked as the ninth-best wide receiver in football — for many of the reasons Byard explained. “He changes the coverages people play, everything will be rolled his way, and it will lighten the box for Josh [McDaniels] to really get the run game going,” a coordinator said. “He gives them run-after-catch explosion and isolation down the field on 50-50 plays that they didn’t have.” Brown joined Drake Maye, Milton Williams and Christian Gonzalez as Patriots players to crack the top 10 at their respective positions. Hunter Henry, TreVeyon Henderson and Kevin Byard also received votes. The Patriots’ representation in the rankings highlights just how much the roster has improved over the last year. At this time last offseason, Gonzalez was the only New England player to appear in ESPN’s positional surveys. ESPYs Drake Maye’s successful sophomore campaign earned him nominations for both Best NFL Player and Best Breakthrough Athlete at the annual ESPY Awards. When the winners were announced Wednesday night, Maye fell short in both categories, with Myles Garrett taking home Best NFL Player honors and Alysa Liu winning Best Breakthrough Athlete. In the Community Before returning to Foxboro for their own work, Patriots players got to work in the community over the past few weeks holding a number of kids camps across the country. That included Christian Gonzalez, Rhamondre Stevenson, Efton Chism III and Kayshon Boutte, Alijah Vera-Tucker, TreVeyon Henderson and more. To end this past week, Drake Maye held three camps with FlexWork Sports in both Massachusetts and New Hampshire. “I told them to ask questions. I’m an open book,” Maye said. “I love pouring into kids lives. I remember being at this age, it’s probably when I started playing football — some of these six year olds. So, I love it.” Forged The Patriots released Season 2, Episode 2 of Forged in Foxborough on Friday. The 28-minute episode covers the early parts of offseason team activities and behind the scenes of acquiring A.J. Brown. Week ahead The Patriots will officially report back to Gillette Stadium this week with rookies and select veterans returning on Wednesday, July 22. Veterans will then follow on Friday, July 24 where head coach Mike Vrabel will then address the media. The first practice of the summer in then Saturday, July 25 beginning at 10:30 a.m. ET. Pats Pulpit will have all your training camp coverage when the team returns to action. In the mean time, we will still provide you with daily coverage, including additional offseason wrap-up coverage, training camp previews, and our roster scouting report series . So, make sure to stay tuned.

View this post on Instagram A second-round draft pick by the Patriots in 2019, Williams appeared in a combined 38 regular season and playoff games for the team. Despite an intriguing athletic profile, he never managed to carve out a regular role on the defensive side of the ball and had his most consistent impact on special teams. As a consequence, the team opted not to re-sign him as a free agent in 2023. Williams subsequently spent time with the Vikings, Bears and Saints, adding six more games to bring his career total to 44. He last played in a game in January 2024, and in May announced his decision to step away from the game. title: Why can’t MetLife Stadium have grass for NFL games?
summary: It had to be galling to New York Giants (and Jets) fans when MetLife Stadium was announced as one of the venues for the 2026 World Cup. Not because fans are protective of their beautiful stadium (which MetLife most certainly is not), but because soccer’s governing body FIFA requires that all matches be played on […]
full_text: It had to be galling to New York Giants (and Jets) fans when MetLife Stadium was announced as one of the venues for the 2026 World Cup . Not because fans are protective of their beautiful stadium (which MetLife most certainly is not), but because soccer’s governing body FIFA requires that all matches be played on a grass pitch rather than artificial turf. Giants fans have been pleading for years for the Mara and Tisch families to replace the infamous turf at MetLife, author of Malik Nabers’ season-ending ACL injury in Game 4 of the 2025 season, with real grass, as so many other NFL stadiums have. It’s fallen on deaf ears…until this year. Money talks, and for several more days, we will see MetLife in all its natural grass glory until the final match between Spain and Argentina is over. FIFA worries about ACL injuries too, because they are fairly common in soccer. One recent study found that there were 1.7 ACL injuries per 10,000 athlete events . This has led to the “ FIFA 11+” injury prevention program. NFL football is different from soccer in the movements and stresses it places on the human body, and unlike the sport-wide FIFA 11+ protocol, injury prevention in the NFL is overseen by individual teams rather than there being a league-wide protocol. A recent study concluded that over a four-year period there were 149 ligament tears in 1213 games played, with the rate being slightly higher on turf (0.132 tears per game) than grass (0.111 tears per game), a statistically insignificant difference. During the World Cup there has been one ACL tear, to Belgium’s Amadou Onana in Belgium’s victory over the US in Seattle. That’s one injury in 102 matches, much lower (0.0098) than the NFL rate. But, small number statistics and different sports. That said, we now have data on whether two NFL teams sharing the same field can support real grass thanks to FIFA’s experiment. I don’t know if the NFL does this for grass fields, but FIFA requires that sod be grown with a plastic layer underneath, which forces roots to spread horizontally and create a dense grass layer. The grass grown by a local sod farm in British Columbia for Vancouver BC Place World Cup matches received rave reviews from players. Alas, the same could not be said for the grass grown for MetLife World Cup matches. After the first two matches, The Athletic reported that: With two matches played there, and six more to come including the final, the condition of the playing surface is already raising concerns. High-profile players such as Brazil star Vinicius Junior and France’s Adrien Rabiot described the pitch as dry and difficult to play on, while Rabiot’s coach Didier Deschamps said it was “special”. (He didn’t mean it in a good way.) Vinicious Junior said that: “Because of the weather and the heat, the grass dries out quickly and the game ends up being very slow. We can’t build up a rhythm,” the Real Madrid player told TNT Sports Brazil. “That makes things difficult because we want to play. We want to move the ball from one side to the other and this disrupts our game. But we have to adapt because I believe it will be like this all tournament. France head coach Didier Deschamps and player Adrien Rabiot called the grass at MetLife Stadium “a special surface — it’s different.” “We need to get used to this. There might be some cement below the grass. You have very short shards of grass here. But we do adjust. This does create a change, but we take these technicalities into account.” Rabiot shared a similar assessment. “Well,” he started, “the pitch was… I don’t know if I’d even call it that. It seemed more like an artificial pitch. It was hard and rigid, but it’s like that for every team. You need to adapt to the conditions. “I hope we find better pitches in our other games.” It didn’t pass the eye test either: From the press box it appears a number of worn patches have developed on the MetLife Stadium pitch after just 1 game, so I went down to investigate. From field level they appear to be minor. The overhead view seems to exaggerate them a bit. We’ll see how it holds up over 8 games pic.twitter.com/s1dbyu6tuV — Kyle Bonn (@the_bonnfire) June 16, 2026 The criticism goes back even to last year when Club World Cup matches were held at MetLife. NFL players overwhelmingly advocate for grass fields, not just because of the injury issue but also due to what they see as increased wear and tear on their bodies overall after games on turf relative to grass: Tomorrow, the World Cup kicks off. Over the course of the tournament, 11 NFL stadiums will host 78 soccer matches on high-quality grass fields installed to meet FIFA demands. When the World Cup ends, many of these same stadiums will go back to turf despite 92% of NFL players… pic.twitter.com/KIh2F6oXKI — NFLPA (@NFLPA) June 10, 2026 But what is it with MetLife specifically? If BC Place and others can do it, why not here? There are a couple of reasons. One is just the luck of the draw as far as weather goes. There are cool season and warm season grasses. For a tournament played in June and July in New Jersey, of course you’d plant a warm season (Bermuda) grass. Just one problem – Mother Nature didn’t get the memo. May was not as consistently warm as expected , and the Bermuda grass didn’t grow fast enough. Unlike BC Place, which used sod from a local grower, MetLife had to have sod trucked in on a 12-hour drive from North Carolina because the planned usage of a local New Jersey supplier was prevented by the Northeast’s harsh winter. That said, MetLife will end up hosting eight World Cup matches matches in a month and a half, more than it will host for the Giants and Jets combined over a similar time period. There’s another factor that is specific to MetLife, though, and this may be the death knell for the hopes of a permanent grass field. Here is the Met Life schedule starting August 1: Aug. 1-2: BTS (Korean boy band, in case like me you had to look them up) Aug 7-6: Chris Brown and Usher Aug. 12: Guns N’ Roses Aug. 14: Jets – Tampa Bay preseason game Aug, 15: Giants – Vikings preseason game Aug, 21, 22, 25, 26: Bruno Mars Aug. 28: Jets – Giants preseason game Sept. 4-5: Ed Sheeran Sept. 11: BigBang (another Korean boy band) Sept. 13: Giants – Cowboys season opener Sept. 17-18: Karol G (Colombian singer, had to look her up, too) Sept. 20: Jets – Packers Sept. 25: AC/DC Sept. 25: Giants – Titans You get the idea. For the next two months, MetLife is going to be packed with events, presumably with tons of people on the field. This, in addition to the cost, may be the real reason that the Giants and Jets are so resistant to going to grass. And regarding that latter point, remember that moving to grass permanently is something that Jets owner Woody Johnson would have to agree to and split the cost for, not just the Maras and Tisches. Perhaps the World Cup was a turning point, though. Maybe some day the owners will finally listen to the players on this issue, and we’ll hear the players shout in unison: “Go-o-o-o-o-o-al!” In the short term, though, don’t expect anything but a yellow card.

title: Is Giants’ QB Jaxson Dart more than just an athletic project?
summary: The New York Giants are betting heavily on quarterback Jaxson Dart. Even with the arrival of John Harbaugh, a revamped defense, and renewed emphasis on the run game, the Giants will go as far as Dart is capable of taking them. Dart’s rookie season was exciting, with flashes of brilliance and even some Mahomesian magic. […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart: Waiver Wire gem in 2025 | Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images The New York Giants are betting heavily on quarterback Jaxson Dart . Even with the arrival of John Harbaugh, a revamped defense, and renewed emphasis on the run game, the Giants will go as far as Dart is capable of taking them. Dart’s rookie season was exciting, with flashes of brilliance and even some Mahomesian magic. But there’s also still plenty of room for improvement in Dart’s game, and national opinions on him are split. For instance, Dart was the 28th-ranked quarterback in SB Nation’s analytics powered preseason quarterback rankings . That put him four spots below Tyler Shough at the bottom of their 4th tier of QBs, just above 2025 first overall pick Cam Ward as the second-worst QB in the second-worst tier. Here’s how Dart graded out on their 6 criteria Offensive impact – 7 Accuracy – 4 Explosive plays – 4 Scoring – 4 Lack of turnovers – 8 Clutch – 4 Overall – 31 Personally, I am both okay saying that Dart is a fourth-tier quarterback, and saying that I don’t put much stock in their rankings. Frankly, I struggle with a piece of analysis that doesn’t show it’s work or explain the methodology: Case in point, Jaxson Dart had 24 total touchdowns in 14 games last year, while Lamar Jackson had 23 total touchdowns in 13 games. Yet, Jackson was given a “10” in scoring, while Dart got a “4”. Of course, the answer is in their “tilt” metric which seems to be there to arm wrestle results into line with popular perception. Known problems with this model: This scoring format naturally hurts quarterbacks with fewer starts in the NFL, because these numbers pull heavily from the 2025 season, with the tilt being evaluated based on career body of work. In reality, Cam Ward and Jaxson Dart should be higher in the rankings — but we just don’t have enough to tilt their rankings up. Similarly, Shedeur Sanders had one of the worst runs as a starter not just in 2025, but in NFL history. This gives him a lot more wiggle room to move up, but it can’t be reflected at this time. But as I said, I’m also okay with saying Dart still has to earn respect league-wide. As things stand now, I’d suggest that the arrow is pointed up, but Dart definitely still needs to work on areas of his game to become a trusted franchise quarterback. Former NFL scout Nate Tice called Dart an “athletic project” when evaluating each of last year’s rookie quarterbacks on the “Football 301” podcast. (You can watch the full podcast below). “My first and foremost takeaway re-watching Jaxson,” Tice said, “and this was my takeaway watching him in college and watching him during his rookie season. “Dude’s a hell of an athlete. Dude is strong. Dude can run. He’s got legit, legit vision. Like, he sets up blocks and he’s willing to chuck some stuff and create some stuff. And that can get him in trouble, which I will get into in a little bit as well. But this guy is a real good athlete and I actually have a comparison for him … that I’m excited to throw out here.” In Tice’s view, Dart has a sky-high upside, but isn’t there yet. Matt Harmon, who joined Tice in evaluating the rookie quarterbacks, pointed to Dart’s advanced stats to show he thrived in chaos, but wasn’t as consistent on a down-to-down basis. “He’s 13th in EPA per play last year, he’s 17th success rate.” Harmon said. “Like, that’s nice. If you just look at pass plays though, then he’s 28th in EPA per drop back on just pass plays. So that’s a part of it like he as you said he should get a lot of leash here. He should get a lot of run cuz the upside is very high. “He is very, very, very, very physically talented … can he progress? “A lot of guys are phenomenal athletes,” Tice said. “I’ll bring up Russ as one of them, but even guys like Justin Fields or something, they have to learn to win from the pocket. They just have to they can keep scrambling and running, but they just have to balance out the numbers. And when he was pressured last year, Dart scrambled 17.1% of the time, which easily led the NFL. 8.8% is the league average for comparison’s sake. Since 2013, that’s the seventh highest rate under pressure by any quarterback to scramble rate under pressure.” Overall, Tice believes that Dart has a “wild horse” mentality that needs to be reined in. It’s a quality that he likes in a quarterback and would rather that than trying to get a cautious passer to cut loose, but it needs to happen nonetheless. “He’s a project,” Tice said. “He’s not to this level, but people should be talking to him more like a Josh Allen than even say, like a Caleb [Williams]. “He’s kind of that, you know Josh Allen is the extreme version of this, but it’s more of a wild horse project that you’re trying to rein in and go from there. So that’s what more of the questions are not playmaking and not like explosive plays. He can do that. It’s just all the filling in between the lines.” Neither Tice nor Matt Harmon would go so far as to say Dart is the next Josh Allen, though the style of quarterback is in that mold. Tice’s comparison, and goal, for Dart is a young Russell Wilson. “He has to become kind of like a version of Russell Wilson when he was young” Tice said. “And I mean that as a scrambler, a hell, like launch that thing down the field, home run swinging quarterback. you take your sacks, you scramble, and you launch stuff. “The thing with Russ that he doesn’t get a lot of credit for was how he could avoid hits. He didn’t really take a lot of big hits.” Tice believes there’s a wide variance in what Dart can become. “It’s how I scout guys and took it from a basketball guy, [is] ‘Star, Starter, Bench, Bust.’ Bench could be average quarterback in in this instance. Like I think Dart has the biggest ‘star’ chunk of that pie [chart], but he has half of it that’s ‘bust’.” However, he also believes that what Dart showed as an explosive playmaker, and the upside to be a star in the league. For comparison, while Tice and Harmon believe that Cam Ward has a high ceiling, and both he and Tyler Shough have higher floors than Dart, neither has as high a ceiling. Chris’ thoughts I do tend to agree with Tice’s evaluation of Dart. I think there’s enough magic in his game to draw comparisons to a young Russell Wilson, particularly considering the baseball background the two share. But there’s also a world in which Dart winds up as a “Justin Fields” who never quite develops and realizes his potential. The structure of the Giants’ offense last year didn’t do Dart a ton of favors, and there were too many plays where his outlets or checkdowns were on the opposite side of the field and well away from his progression in the intended passing concept. But even so, I believe the biggest lever Dart and the Giants can pull to spark his improvement will be — as Tice and Harmon said — learning how to win from the pocket. Dart’s ability to gash defenses with his legs is a dangerous weapon, but it shouldn’t be a weapon of first resort. Personally, I believe Dart will take a significant step forward when he improves his footwork to better time the play and throw with better mechanics. So much will fall into place when his timing and eyes are in sync with the receivers’ routes. Likewise, his accuracy and velocity will improve with a consistent power base for his passes. All of that should make him much more comfortable in the pocket and less likely to scramble at a moment’s notice. He should have the green light to scramble and defenses should have to respect the quarterback running game. Becoming a more discerning runner will help keep him on the field to get the reps he needs to improve, and becoming a more consistent passer will put defenses in the same kind of “pick your poison” situation as when they play Josh Allen or Lamar Jackson. Overall, Dart is definitely better than the 28th quarterback in the NFL. But while he has the potential to reach into the upper echelons of NFL quarterback play, he has work to do in order to get…

full_text: Jan 10, 2026; Charlotte, NC, USA; Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young (9) reflects before an NFC Wild Card Round game at Bank of America Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Bob Donnan-Imagn Images | Bob Donnan-Imagn Images When and where: Week 6 at home Key additions: EDGE Jaelen Phillips, LB Devin Lloyd Key subtractions: C Cade Mayes, DT A’Shawn Robinson, RB, Rico Dowdle Last season: Were the second team in four years to win the NFC South with an 8-9 record The question for this team: Is this team any good? Do they even care? The rules say that every division has to have a “winner”, and the 8-9 Carolina Panthers, who lost in Week 18 to an imploding Buccaneers team, were deemed the winner of the NFC South. Congratulations. They nearly beat the Rams in the playoffs, which might have said more about the Rams (who then needed OT to beat the Bears) than it did the Panthers. Bryce Young kind of looked like an NFL QB in 2025, but the Panthers scored just 11 more points than the Jets. The only thing the Panthers excelled at last year was shortening every game. The offense was last in number of drives, 22nd in number of offensive snaps (which helped their defense face the 9th fewest plays against), 21st in pass attempts, 27th in yards per attempt, with Bryce Young 30th among 33 qualified QBs in Intended Air Yards Per Attempt. The 2025 Panthers were not really interested in actually trying to play football. The 2026 team doesn’t seem to be either. Tet McMillian was the only Panther with more than 400 receiving yards, Carolina’s biggest additions to their WR room were John Metchie and his 686 career yards, and a Josh Heupel WR. Devin Lloyd and Jaelen Phillips (when he’s healthy) should improve the defense, but this is an offense that scored fewer than 14 points seven times last year. You’d need the 1985 Bears defense to win with that kind of output. While the Panthers did pick up Bryce Young’s fifth year option, putting him under contract for 2027 for a guaranteed $26M, they are–correctly–not expected to sign him to a contract extension this offseason. The Carolina Panthers are just going through the motions, knowing that they are going to need a new QB but not in a position to get one, and in a division where even a half assed effort can get you a home playoff game. But months away from this game, we can point to it being a “trap” game. This game is a week after the Eagles play in London, and a week before hosting the Cowboys. The NFL usually gives teams a bye after flying back from Europe, over the past three years 16 teams had a bye while 11 did not. Over the past two seasons jet lagged teams went 2-5. But in 2023 they went 4-0, so it’s not a Herculean challenge to overcome. Meanwhile, the Panthers will be coming off their bye. This is pretty unfair scheduling.

summary: We’re less than a week away from the first Seattle Seahawks training camp practice. full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - AUGUST 07: Jacardia Wright #31 of the Seattle Seahawks carries the ball during the third quarter of the NFL Preseason 2025 game against Las Vegas Raiders at Lumen Field on August 7, 2025 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jane Gershovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re less than a week away from the first Seattle Seahawks training camp practice. Rookies have already reported as of Friday, with everyone else set to return to Virginia Mason Athletic Center on July 24. The first of 10 public practices will be held on July 25, and don’t bother looking for tickets because that opening session is already sold out. Having taken a look at roster bubble players last week , our training camp preview continues by focusing on three Seahawks who ended last season on the practice squad but might just have a golden opportunity to go from “ready squad” to the active roster. Jacardia Wright, Running Back As noted in the roster bubble article, there will be a different Seahawks backfield to start the season. Kenneth Walker is elsewhere, Zach Charbonnet is likely going to start on the PUP list, and one of the main backs added to the team is first-round pick Jadarian Price. George Holani and Emanuel Wilson probably are safe bets to join Price on the 53-man roster, but if there’s room for a fourth running back—again, that might only be a necessity for as long as Charbonnet is out—Kenny McIntosh has some company to deal with. Wright was one of the preseason standouts last season after signing as an undrafted free agent out of Missouri State. He showed good lateral movement and vision during camp and in actual games, and he had a few touches as a practice squad call-up against the New Orleans Saints. An ankle injury shut his season down early, although I suspect he was more or less stashed to avoid getting poached/free up a PS spot. Falling in love with the UDFA running back or receiver is like a time-honored tradition for Seahawks fans. I’ve no expectations for Wright’s ceiling to be anything other than a good reserve, but this is as good a chance as any for him to stake his claim to at least be on the Week 1 roster. Chris Paul Jr, Inside Linebacker ‘Pooh’ Paul was drafted in the fifth round by the Los Angeles Rams, surprisingly waived at the end of preseason, and promptly scooped up by the Seahawks. Hey, the pain of being let go as a rookie can be eased by having a Super Bowl ring. We have no actual data on Paul in a Seahawks uniform because, well, he never got on the field. But based on what he showcased at Arkansas and Ole Miss, where he earned second-team All-SEC honors, there is promise and hope that he can do something at an NFL level. Ernest Jones and Drake Thomas are the starting inside linebackers, so there’s nothing to debate there. The reserves consist of Tyrice Knight, Chazz Surratt and Patrick O’Connell. Surratt is mostly a special teams guy, whereas O’Connell has spent much of his career as a practice squad player. Unless there is reason to believe Knight has completely fallen out of favor, Paul has a chance to sneak in as Seattle’s fourth off-ball backer. Jamie Sheriff, Outside Linebacker The Sheriff has been in town for a couple of years, playing on special teams in his two career appearances. He flashed as a promising edge rushing talent during 2024 preseason, so much so that the Carolina Panthers gave him a look after Seattle waived him. Sheriff was let go shortly after Week 1 of his rookie campaign and has remained with the Seahawks ever since. There was talk last year about Sheriff working with the off-ball linebackers, but everything I saw at training camp indicated that he was doing a hell of a lot of work at the line of scrimmage. If there was an effort to at least make him a hybrid backer, it didn’t really take off through preseason. Sheriff’s best ability is getting after the quarterback. Boye Mafe’s departure is effectively offset by the signing of Dante Fowler Jr, but after Messrs Nwosu, Lawrence, Hall, and Fowler, it’s up for grabs in terms of a fifth (or even sixth) edge rusher. Jared Ivey is one of those bigger edge players who could sooner move positions than anything else, Connor O’Toole will be in the mix after a special teams-heavy workload last season, Aidan Hubbard and Marvin Jones Jr are intriguing UDFA rookies, so there’s quite a bit of competition to face. Jamie Sheriff has been an easy story to root for, so it would be nice for him to make a splash in camp and preseason and really stake a claim for a promotion to the 53. Honorable Mention: Tyrone Broden, Cornerback Switching from wide receiver to cornerback is nothing new, especially not to the Seahawks. None of the previous converts was 6’7 like Tyrone Broden. Is it likely to work out? Almost certainly not. Will it at least be interesting to watch? Sure! Biggest storyline: The Titans are essentially running it back with Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears. There have been some back-end changes but make no mistake, the rushing attack will go as far as Pollard and Spears are capable of carrying them. An improved passing offense, spearheaded by Cam Ward and Brian Daboll, could have a positive impact on the ground-and-pound approach. Most to prove: Spears is entering a contract year. He’s missed a handful of contests in consecutive seasons as lingering issues muted his impact across 2024 and 2025. The fanbase is excited about sixth-round rookie Nicholas Singleton. Singleton displayed explosiveness and athleticism at Penn State. Mullings disappointed as a rookie, but also has special teams upside as a former linebacker. Carter previously played for Saleh and has the closest skill set to Spears, if the Titans need insurance there given his history of injuries.

summary: This article will not take a deeper look at Athan Kaliakmanis’ nicknames, of which there are several, including “the Greek Rifle” and “Golden Boy.” Instead, we will focus on what makes the selection of the former Rutgers QB in the seventh round a good decision. Mandatory Credit: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images | Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images This article will not take a deeper look at Athan Kaliakmanis’ nicknames, of which there are several, including “the Greek Rifle” and “Golden Boy.” Instead, we will focus on what makes the selection of the former Rutgers QB in the seventh round a good decision. Following the conclusion of the 2026 NFL draft, there were several analysts that disagreed with this premise, assigning Adam Peters’ final pick an overall “C-” grade. 2026 NFL Draft grades for every NFC East team 🧵 📊 Commanders: A+ LB Sonny Styles (7): A WR Antonio Williams (71): A+ EDGE Joshua Josephs (147): A+ RB Kaytron Allen (187): B+ C Matt Gulbin (209): B+ QB Athan Kaliakmanis (223): C- pic.twitter.com/g75smXtakK — Pro Football Network (@PFN365) May 7, 2026 My Commanders draft grades: Round 1 (7): Sonny Styles – A+ Round 3 (71): Antonio Williams B Round 5 (147): Joshua Josephs A Round 6 (187): RB Kaytron Allen B+ Round 6 (209): Matt Gulbin B Round 7 (223): Athan Kaliakmanis C- — Tiller56 (@Tiller56) April 25, 2026 Reasons for the poor grade varied, but most of the criticism centered around a perceived lack of need, the opinion that there were better options still available, and that Kaliakmanis’ overall body of work in college was not impressive. Let’s address each item separately. The need at the position might not be readily apparent to some as Marcus Mariota returns for a third season to back up Jayden Daniels. Generally viewed as one of the better QB2s in the league, Mariota has seen far more game action than most would prefer. In the first season, Marcus proved his worth early, taking over for an injured Daniels in the team’s matchup versus the Carolina Panthers and skillfully leading the team to a 40-7 victory. More importantly, he came into the last game of the season to guide the team in a comeback win versus the Cowboys and clinched the 6th seed in the NFC playoffs for the Commanders with a last-second throw to Terry McLaurin. Things started to unravel when Mariota was pressed into service the second half of last season, starting eight games with a 2-6 win-loss record. While the team had already been decimated by injuries by the time Mariota started the majority of his games, his play slowly deteriorated over the course of the season, and Marcus’ decision-making in London’s Miami game was questionable. Turning 33 years old in October and still commanding one of the highest backup quarterback salaries in the league, Washington may look to go in another direction in 2027. While another veteran is always an option, a younger player with potential to grow along with David Blough would be preferable. The Commanders coaching staff signaled that Sam Hartman was not that player when they opted to go with Josh Johnson at the end of the season. So what makes Athan the choice over other options that were available at the tail end of the draft, including Garrett Nussmeier or Haynes King? Kaliakmanis doesn’t distinguish himself in the size or athleticism categories, with okay to good ratings in most categories and a poor one for speed. Athan Kaliakmanis was drafted in round 7 with pick 223 in the 2026 draft class. He scored a 5.37 RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 523 out of 1128 QB from 1987 to 2026. https://t.co/i2lhw1snUY pic.twitter.com/mEnHvsNTmG — RAS.football (@MathBomb) April 25, 2026 Athan certainly doesn’t have the mobility of a Haynes King ( RAS 9.61 ) or the arm of Nussmeier, and his performance under pressure is a work in progress. He does have demonstrated rhythm and timing with a quick release along with the ability to challenge all three levels of defense, which makes him a good fit for David Blough’s proposed offense. The arm strength might not be elite, but Kaliakmanis throws an extremely accurate deep ball with a nice trajectory to match his wide receivers downfield. Athan Kaliakmanis is one of the best QBs in the country pic.twitter.com/GfVtVPsQgC — NFL Draft Files (@NFL_DF) September 23, 2025 Can’t wait to watch Athan KaliakManis play again pic.twitter.com/M3NmAI1USV — CFBTalkDaily (@CFBTalkDaily) May 15, 2025 His accuracy is inconsistent, as is his ball placement, so what made the Washington Commanders invest a draft pick in him over other options? Potential. Specifically, potential at the most important position in the game. Athan doesn’t have the college resume of a Garret Nussmeier or the playmaking ability of Haynes King, but what he does have is untapped potential. Kaliakmanis wasn’t even a starter at Minnesota until his third year in college, but he demonstrated a decidedly linear progression after transferring to Rutgers. His decision-making, production, and even his arm strength increased exponentially. Athan’s completion rate jumped from 53.9% in 2024 to 62.2% in 2025, a significant leap that coincided with 20 touchdowns against only seven interceptions. His PFSN College QB Impact score has increased every season, resulting in a career-high 82.2 score in his final campaign. The intangibles are there as well. Kaliakmanis has a high football IQ and understanding of the game and called his own pass protections on the field. He has the ability to go through full-field progressions if given the necessary time. Athan is considered a plus culture fit, and the Commanders decided to bring him in for a Top 30 visit . David Blough is now the offensive coordinator , replacing Kliff Kingsbury, while running back Rachaad White and tight end Chig Okonkwo have been brought in as younger reinforcements for Austin Ekeler and Zach Ertz. Establishing the run will be a point of emphasis in Blough’s scheme, as well as getting his tight ends involved and using creativity in his play design. Still, there will be hurdles to overcome. The Commanders remain without a proven WR2 after the Brandon Aiyuk rumors seem to have fallen through . Blough has never been an offensive coordinator before, and there’s no guarantee he pans out. If Washington is to return to the playoffs, much of the responsibility will fall on Daniels to be the savior he was drafted to be. With the amount of roster change that NFL teams undergo annually along with the unusually large number of head coach and coordinator changes in 2026, it seems useful to spend some time to review each of Washington’s regular season opponents. FALCONS This Week 15 game pits two teams that have close ties, starting with the fact that Dan Quinn’s first head coaching job was with the Falcons, and that he has a long history with the Falcons defensive coordinator, Jeff Ulbrich, who — if he’d been released by the Falcons when Raheem Morris was fired earlier this calendar year — might well have been hired as Washington’s 2026 DC. Quinn coached Ulbrich when the latter was a linebacker for the 49ers in the 2000s. Quinn then helped Ulbrich land his first NFL coaching gig in Seattle (2010) and later hired him onto his Falcons coaching staff in 2015. Now, the student and his former teacher will face off in a late-season NFC battle. Week 15 Preview: Atlanta Falcons at Washington Commanders Date: December 20, 2026, 1:00 p.m. ET Location: Northwest Stadium in Landover, Maryland First-year head coaches have a notoriously poor track record, as they tend to be in charge of a team with a transitioning roster in an organization that is trying to change the culture. Kevin Stefanski, however, is nobody’s NFL rookie coach. After 14 years with the Vikings, he was hired as head coach of the Browns in 2020, where he coached for 6 seasons before being sacked in January. His tenure was a bit of everything — a pair of 11-win seasons; a pair of seasons with 8 & 7 wins; and just 8 wins in his final two seasons combined (‘24 & ‘25). Despite his overall record of 45-56 as a head coach (1-2 in the playoffs), Stefanski’s lack of on-field success is attributed by many observers to the fact that he was coaching in Cleveland, where things were stacked against him. The Browns franchise went 13 years without a winning season before Stefanski delivered an 11-5 record as a rookie head coach in 2020. In 2023, his team went 11-6 and he was named AP Coach of the Year. The miserable two years leading to Stefanski getting fired may have had a lot to do with the roster he was given and the general disarray that seems to always define the Browns franchise. Remember that Deshaun Watson was his “franchise quarterback” since being signed to a historically bad contract in 2022. In Atlanta, Stefanski arrives with longtime Ravens & Eagles front office executive and now General Manager, Ian Cunningham. It is a fresh start in a franchise whose owner, Arthur Blank, is hungry for a Lombardi Trophy, and who is known for doing everything possible to help his team succeed. This offseason, the Falcons signed Tua Tagovailoa to a rock-bottom contract of $1.215m (with roughly $53m being paid to the QB by his former team, the Miami Dolphins because of his contract guarantees). This gives Steafanski two former 1st-round picks at the QB position, with Michael Penix Jr, drafted in 2024, returning from a mid-November ACL tear suffered last season. The Falcons were 5-3 with Kirk Cousins starting 8 games a year ago (including the final 4 games of the season, and 5 of 7 starts after Penix’ injury), but 3-6 when Penix was the starter. Cousins, of course, is now a Raider, living in Las Vegas, which seems slightly out of character for someone of his temperament. The point is that the Falcons have the roster talent to win games under the right leadership, and by Week 15 of the upcoming season, the Falcons will likely either be very much in the playoff race or very much out of it. My bet is that this game against the Commanders will be a critical one for both teams’ playoff hopes, with the winner staying alive and the loser starting to prepare for the 2027 draft — very much like 2024, when a 30-24 overtime win by Washington propelled the Commanders to the playoffs while the Falcons finished the season with a losing record. Commanders fans will recognize at least two names on the Atlanta roster. Former Commanders 1st-round pick Jahan Dotson is a Falcon now, and WR Olamide Zaccheaus , who spent the ‘24 season in Washington with his former head coach, has returned to Atlanta, where he played his first four NFL seasons from 2019-22. As you’ll read in the next section that details the all-time series between the two teams, the Falcons and Commanders know each other very well, and have played one another frequently — at least in recent years. The All-Time Series Numbers The Washington Redskins used to be perceived as ‘the team of the South’ in the early- to mid-20th century. NFL football had started as primarily a sport concentrated in the northeast and northern midwest. By relocating from Boston to Washington in 1937, the Redskins became the default ‘home’ team for a large swath of the country that had no true home team to root for. That changed when the Falcons took the field in Atalanta in 1966. Suddenly, there was competition for regional football fans. Unsurprisingly, the Redskins dominated the competition against the expansion team for many years. Washington was 5-0-1 vs the Falcons in the first 12 years of the rivalry, and 15-4-1 through the 2003 season. From 2006 to 2018, the teams played 6 times, with the Falcons winning every game — a perfect 6-0 against Joe Gibbs, Jim Zorn, Mike Shanahan and Jay Gruden! Unusually, since 2021, Washington and Atlanta have played each other in the regular season each year — 2026 will mark the 6th straight season the two teams have played each other, and it has mostly gone Washington’s way during that time. The burgundy & gold won the first 4 meetings before losing to the Falcons in Week 4 last year — an early sign that Dan Quinn & Jayden Daniels’ 2nd season was not going to plan. Overall, Washington holds a commanding 19-11-1 lead in the series which can be broken up into three distinct stages: 15-4-1 from ‘66 to ‘03; 0-6 from ‘06 to ’18; and 4-1 since 2021. The two teams have met in the playoffs only once — the NFC Divisional round following the 1991 season. Washington, as you may already know, won that game 24-7 and went on to win Super Bowl XXVI. But, then, that was the greatest NFL team in history . This season’s Week 15 clash shouldn’t be seen as just a likely late-season playoff push; it should represent an intellectual chess match in which Dan Quinn and his staff try to out-maneuver a defensive system run by Ulbrich that Quinn himself helped pioneer and foster for over a decade, dating back to the days in Seattle when Ulbrich worked for Quinn.
